name: Flexible-load services
desc: Treatment of loads that agree to curtail or be dispatched, and the faster study and services they earn in return.

letters.desc: AEMA's central proposal is a dedicated Flexible Load Fast Track giving loads that make verifiable flexibility commitments an expedited 60-to-90-day study process. Flexibility must be defined in performance-based, technology-neutral terms covering temporal, spatial, resource, and adjacent flexibility, with bounded upper limits on curtailment obligations so operators have investment certainty.
quotes: AEMA urges the Commission to create a Flexible Load Fast Track (FLFT) for facilities that can verifiably adjust their consumption in response to system conditions and harness a broad set of technologies to deliver flexibility to the grid.

The FLFT would be an expedited (60-90 day) interconnection process for loads that commit to flexibility and would incorporate this flexibility into studies that determine whether transmission grid upgrades are necessary to interconnect the load.

The Commission should direct transmission providers to treat this verifiable reduction as equivalent to a system-impact mitigation, allowing such projects to be studied and interconnected on a shorter timeline.

AEMA recommends that the interconnection study process be used to define clear, upper-bound limits on the required flexibility (e.g., maximum number of hours per year, hours per event, depth of flexibility, and events per year) needed to mitigate specific system constraints.

The final rule should remain strictly technology-neutral, focusing not on the method used, but on the measurable, verifiable, and reliable performance of the resources at their point of interconnection.

Under this model, the operator issues a dispatch signal, for example a 100-megawatt curtailment request to the facility's registered energy management interface. The facility's flexibility management platform executes the reduction automatically and provides real-time or near-real-time, auditable telemetry back to the operator to confirm compliance.
Fast-acting load adjustments can reduce the frequency of local congestion events, defer transmission upgrades, and moderate wholesale price volatility.

AEMA believes the FLFT provides a crucial, market-based choice for large loads: (1) interconnect as an inflexible load and potentially bear the costs for the resulting, often slow and expensive, network upgrades; or (2) interconnect as a flexible load via the FLFT, avoid triggering those upgrades, and get online faster at lower cost. This protects all other ratepayers from socializing upgrade costs.
Coordinate with NERC (Principle 14) to establish uniform telemetry and performance reporting standards, which can enable the 'verifiable' aspect of the FLFT.

letters.desc: AEMA supports a Flexible Load Fast Track that accepts any combination of storage, software, thermal, or on-site generation as long as it delivers verifiable flexibility. The filing argues that a performance-based, technology-neutral approach is faster, cheaper, and more reliable than prescribing a single pathway. Curtailable loads monitored in real time provide reliability services physically equivalent to generation.
quotes: AEMA urges the Commission to adopt an expressly 'all-of-the-above' approach in which any particular technology (whether storage, thermal resources, on-site generation, or software-defined controls) or combination thereof is encouraged so long as it can verifiably deliver the flexibility attributes that support reliability.

The fastest way to connect new loads that advances affordability, effectively drives investment into U.S. competitiveness and AI infrastructure rapidly, and bolsters grid reliability is to harness the full suite of flexibility technologies in a technology-neutral and performance-based way.

flexible load capabilities should be leveraged to bridge the gap between immediate interconnection needs and the longer timelines required for traditional transmission upgrades, accelerating AI infrastructure investments while also deferring or avoiding upgrades that can raise costs for ratepayers.

AEMA strongly urges the Commission to reject arguments from the Independent Market Monitor for PJM ("PJM IMM"), the Electric Power Supply Association ("EPSA"), the Illinois Attorney General, and others suggesting that large loads must "bring their own generation" or that demand-side solutions are inferior to generation assets.
AEMA urges the Commission to treat generation matching as one optional pathway among many to achieve flexibility, not as a mandatory precondition for timely interconnection.
When a large load commits to a tariff-backed operational limit—monitored in real-time by the grid operator—it provides a reliability service physically equivalent to generation.

It is a fundamental principle of interconnection policy that customers who impose different impacts on the system should be treated differently. A load that is legally and technically bound to curtail during constraints does not require the same network upgrades as a static, inflexible load.

a final rule singling out loads or hybrid facilities that pair matching generation as the sole mechanism for expedited interconnection—while excluding verifiable load flexibility—would be unduly discriminatory.

letters.desc: The filing expands the ANOPR flexibility principle beyond on-site curtailment to include loads that contract with off-site demand response or distributed resources. It proposes non-firm transmission access as an additional incentive, and asks that curtailable large loads not displace existing demand response programs.
quotes: United agrees with the underlying logic that curtailment and/or dispatch of load and hybrid facilities supports 'the timely and orderly addition of large loads to the transmission system in a safe, reliable, and non-discriminatory manner.' However, this principle applies more broadly, and should be expanded to realize the full benefits of load flexibility to accommodate rapid growth of new large loads.

New large loads willing to operate without firm transmission access—either permanently on a temporary basis as network upgrades are planned and constructed—should have clearly defined, optional, and expedited pathways to do so.

letters.desc: AES prefers financial mechanisms (incentives, penalties for deviations) over physical limitations on injection and withdrawal rights for co-located facilities, arguing that physical constraints are costly and unnecessarily restrictive.
quotes: Commission should explore other incentives without the need for physical limitations that effectively island large quantities of new generation.
Financial mechanisms to encourage certain behavior or account for deviations, without the need for potentially costly additional system protection equipment, should also be considered.

letters.desc: Alliant Energy supports curtailment-based expedited treatment but opposes standardized demand response program mandates. Bilateral agreements that reflect each customer's operational constraints and grid needs are preferred, allowing participation without rigid program requirements that could deter innovative load management.
quotes: curtailable large loads should not be required to participate in a mandatory formal demand response program as it would unnecessarily hinder and discourage innovative solutions.
Alliant Energy recommends that the Commission allow for flexible, bilateral agreements between large load customers and transmission providers.

letters.desc: Amazon Energy favors solutions that give customers and businesses the most flexibility in how large loads interconnect, including co-location among the available options.
quotes: Amazon Energy supports solutions that provide the most flexibility to meet the needs of customers and businesses, which can include co-location.

letters.desc: ACP supports regional flexibility and existing stakeholder-led initiatives, including load-generation pairings in SPP and PJM. Federal action should not deter or supplant proactive regional efforts.
quotes: several regions are already moving forward with their own, stakeholder-led approaches to large load interconnection, including pairing load and generation. The Commission should ensure that any action in this proceeding supports regional flexibility, and does not deter or supplant proactive regional efforts

letters.desc: ACC advocates for rules that allow any technology or approach to meet curtailment and flexibility goals rather than prescribing specific solutions. This enables developers to choose the most effective methods for their projects.
quotes: Maintain technology-neutral rules that are flexible and allow a variety of approaches and technologies to meet curtailment or hybrid-facility requirements.

letters.desc: AEP supports a connect-and-manage pathway modeled on ERCOT, where generators can interconnect on an energy-only basis subject to curtailment risk and then progress to full network resource status as proactive transmission planning provides supporting infrastructure. It would eliminate the ERIS-only dead end so all generators are on a pathway to capacity status.
quotes: AEP supports the application of a 'connect and manage' approach (in tandem with other reforms, such as the entry fee model for generator interconnection described below) as a practical solution for the timely interconnection of generation.
Under this approach, all generators pay an entry fee and can rapidly connect to the grid subject to curtailment until supporting network transmission is planned and constructed.

letters.desc: AEP endorses offering conditional or non-firm transmission service to large loads and co-located generators as a short-term bridge until full network upgrades are complete. Customers willing to accept curtailment could come online faster, but terms must protect reliability and ensure fair cost payment.
quotes: Temporary conditional service is a short-term speed-to-power solution that can bring new generation and load on line quickly and be used as a bridge service until the transmission system is upgraded to support full network service to those interconnections.
If large loads are willing to accept conditional transmission service and be curtailed, the Commission could adopt rules that allow LSEs to bring large loads online faster.
Short-term, flexible approaches can facilitate speed-to-power, but they cannot ensure a transmission system that can support the projected large load growth.

letters.desc: The filer centers its proposal on flexible loads, arguing off-peak capacity could host 100 GW and that grid-responsive data centers can throttle GPU power to curtail roughly half their draw without stopping workloads. It urges FERC to define qualifying flexible loads and regulate them rather than leaving the matter to individual grid operators.
quotes: American Terawatt urges the Commission to focus swiftly and pragmatically on reforms that can be adopted without delay and that will encourage the timely expansion of digital and energy infrastructure.

Existing off-peak grid capacity could accommodate an additional 100 GW of flexible loads, more than enough to cover data-center growth and other demand through 2028 and beyond, without needing new power plants.
by throttling GPU power and slowing computations rather than switching devices off entirely, grid-responsive AI data centers (GRAIDs) can maintain uptime SLAs without ever stopping workloads.
Including facility overhead, a 100-megawatt (MW) GRAIDs facility could curtail approximately 50 MW on demand, all while keeping workloads continuously running.

Data-center developers willing to build flexible AI factories or retrofit existing sites with flexible load capabilities should have access to a significantly accelerated grid interconnection process.
The Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) has so far explicitly chosen not to regulate flexible loads, leaving them to individual grid operators. It’s time for that to change.
FERC should direct independent system operators (ISOs) to develop expedited interconnection processes for defined large flexible loads, with transparent criteria.

FERC should direct regional transmission organizations and ISOs to propose enabling, nondiscriminatory tariffs for participation in expedited interconnection processes for defined large flexible loads.

To ensure clarity for both developers and grid operators and prevent a national patchwork of regulations, FERC should define qualifying flexible loads for the purposes of transmission-level interconnection and wholesale market participation.

letters.desc: ATC consistently argues that flexibility is the most effective enabler of timely large-load interconnection. It supports a policy statement rather than binding rules, and asks that any requirements be narrowly tailored so transmission owners can continue using existing processes for conforming loads.
quotes: efficient and expeditious interconnection of large loads is no longer merely a commercial preference, but a matter of national security and an economic development imperative.
A "one-size-fits-all" approach could inadvertently hinder progress by upending established processes and increasing the risk of implementation delays.
ATC supports commenters recommending that the Commission consider adopting a policy statement or general guidance rather than a sweeping rule.
requirements should be narrowly tailored to focus on experienced issues and allow maximum flexibility.
the Commission should consider adopting threshold applicability requirements based upon specific operating characteristics.

Limiting applicability to the subset of loads that do not meet with certain operating criteria could provide adequate controls, ensure reliability, contain costs, while preserving the flexibility for transmission owners such as ATC to continue to interconnect traditional, conforming loads based upon our existing interconnection processes.

letters.desc: Antora's central ask is that FERC require all transmission providers to offer permanent, long-term non-firm transmission service for fully curtailable, price-responsive loads, available whether or not the load is co-located. It argues existing models harm flexible loads by treating them like inflexible firm loads, and that load flexibility increases grid utilization and lowers rates.
quotes: load flexibility can critically help to address the challenge of large load growth by increasing transmission and generation capacity utilization, putting downward pressure on rates, and by allowing the grid to accommodate new loads while infrastructure to serve them is being built.

existing service models sharply constrain the commercial viability of flexible load development, and in particular development of highly flexible loads like TES, by treating them the same as inflexible loads.

Antora urges the Commission, in crafting its remedy in this proceeding, to go beyond these recent reforms to require all transmission providers to: (1) offer permanent non-firm transmission service; (2) at rates reflecting actual use that is consistent with cost causation principles; (3) with curtailment requirements for non-firm load integrated into the interconnection study process and resource adequacy requirements.

Highly flexible large loads face substantial interconnection barriers where, as in SPP, the RTO requires a one-to-one matching of non-coincident peak demand with new Designated Network Resources (DNRs).
An artificial DNR requirement is prohibitively expensive, unnecessary given the real-world operation of curtailable large loads like TES, and acts as a roadblock to new beneficial flexible loads.
MISO allows large loads that do not increase the coincident peak to interconnect without new capacity requirements.

FERC should require all jurisdictional RTOs and transmission providers to move quickly to develop and implement similar viable interconnection pathways and affordable (based on cost causation) service for large, flexible and curtailable loads.

Requiring such loads to procure generation capacity as though they consume around the clock yields unjust and unreasonable costs, contradicts cost-causation principles, and unduly discriminates against such loads by treating differently-situated customers the same.
CHILLS is conditional and temporary, only available for a seven-year term, after which the customer must transition to firm service.

CHILLS' temporary structure mirrors the Interim NITS product that the Commission required PJM to establish in its recent Co-Location Order, but does not fill the additional need the Commission identified in that proceeding, for the transmission provider to offer a permanent non-firm transmission service option.

Antora proposed an hourly utilization-based rate. This would preserve revenue from high load-factor customers while letting low load-factor loads pay only for the service they use, but this approach was not adopted for CHILLS.
PALS would create a long-term, non-firm transmission service enabling flexible, price-sensitive loads to interconnect without matching capacity.

Non-Firm Transmission Charges: Per-MWh billing at hourly non-firm rates (Zonal Annual Transmission Revenue Requirement/Transmission Zone Peak Load/8760) reflect the true cost causation profile of curtailable loads; directly supporting NITS costs reduction for existing ratepayers.
this service should be available to any customer capable of meeting the necessary withdrawal limitations, whether or not co-located.
every jurisdictional RTO and transmission owner should be required to offer comparable, permanent, cost-causation-based non-firm service for flexible loads.

letters.desc: Arevia supports expedited treatment for hybrid facilities with generation components capable of curtailment and dispatch.
quotes: If the generating component of the hybrid facility is capable of being curtailable and/or dispatchable, then the combined load and generation facilities should be expedited.

letters.desc: Bloom supports expedited studies but opposes limiting them to curtailable and dispatchable facilities. Any hybrid facility where primary power covers 100% of peak load should also qualify, because network upgrades are unlikely in that case.
quotes: Bloom urges the Commission to expand expedited studies to include hybrid facilities having primary power sufficient to meet its peak load.

The ANOPR seemingly takes the position that agreement by a hybrid facility to be dispatchable and curtailable is the "grand bargain" for expedited interconnection studies, but it should not be the only way to receive expedited studies.

letters.desc: Load flexibility, including hybrid facilities with generation or storage, should be studied and treated as a cost-effective alternative to traditional transmission upgrades. Customers must be able to propose flexibility solutions to defer or avoid infrastructure needs if they commit to performance during identified constraint periods.
quotes: Require that the transmission owners and RTO/ISOs study load flexibility (including hybrid configurations of load including generation or energy storage) as part of the load interconnection process and identify the amount of flexibility needed to avoid each system constraint identified in the study.

Provide a pathway for large load customers to propose, develop, and implement load flexibility solutions (including hybrid configurations of load including generation or energy storage) to defer or avoid the need for, some or all, new infrastructure if the customer commits to providing flexibility during the hours or system conditions identified during the study process. Load flexibility solutions should be considered on equal footing to traditional infrastructure solutions in system planning processes.

The wholesale markets have offered a place for customers to bring creative solutions to meet the system's needs cost-effectively. While this marketplace for innovation is available for many market services, a similar opportunity for transmission service does not exist for load customers because of the inflexible and opaque way in which load connection studies are conducted.

The Commission should ensure that the study process reflects the expected operating characteristics of the generation (or energy storage) and the load. The study process should provide a pathway for load and hybrid facilities to request that flexibility and specific operating characteristics be incorporated into study assumptions. Solutions that incorporate load flexibility (including hybrid configurations of load including generation or energy storage) should be treated on equal footing as traditional transmission infrastructure solutions.

letters.org: California Department of Water Resources State Water Project
letters.desc: DWR favors enabling load to bid into real-time markets and participate in demand response rather than offering a one-time queue jump. DWR cites its own 2,600 MW of curtailable SWP pumping load as an example of existing curtailable capacity that market tools could unlock at no additional ratepayer cost.
quotes: The Commission should not establish expedited study treatment for large loads that agree to be curtailable, due to the potential for discriminatory access and increased costs to ratepayers.

Instead, the Commission should adopt market-based approaches to encourage load—both new and existing—to be curtailable, which will mitigate undue discrimination concerns and more fully unlock the benefits of curtailable load.
Expedited study treatment is a less effective means of unlocking the benefits of curtailable load, because it is a one-time incentive that would only apply to new large load interconnection requests.

If CAISO implements real-time load bidding, DWR can provide approximately 2,600 MW of available curtailable load, because the State Water Project's water pumping operations are curtailable in response to market signals.
Unlocking the curtailability of existing loads requires no upgrades or increased ratepayer costs—it simply requires new market functionality.

letters.desc: CAISO supports using curtailability and dispatchability as the basis for expedited interconnection. It recommends a tiered lane system so that only fully curtailable facilities receive the most expedited treatment, preserving reliability incentives.
quotes: The CAISO recommends that any final rule should establish distinct 'lanes' based on the level of dispatch tools the transmission provider will have--all, some, or none.

being curtailable on some hours or on some days or for only a portion of the load or generating capacity should not allow a facility to avail itself of the same expedited process as completely curtailable facilities.

letters.desc: If the Commission proceeds, the CPUC urges flexible guidelines rather than prescriptive rules. State and regional differences, evolving technology, and the diversity of large load customers mean that a one-size-fits-all rule would be counterproductive and slow energization.
quotes: flexibility and deference to states within their domains would benefit ratepayers, utilities, and industry alike.  Otherwise, the ANOPR's efforts may be counterproductive to the mutual goal of promptly energizing AI data centers.
flexible guidelines would be more effective than cumbersome rules.

"Any standardized procedures dealing with large load interconnection, including any efforts to address the costs of studying these customers, must be flexible enough to account for the evolving understanding of just what is necessary to integrate these customers to the grid."

letters.desc: The Center endorses demand response and load flexibility for data centers. Research shows that cutting load by just 0.5 percent (44 hours per year) could accommodate 98 GW of new load without new generation, saving ratepayers from subsidizing fossil plants.
quotes: we support Opening Comments urging the Commission to consider the opportunities for these facilities to help mitigate their demand on the grid, by promoting load flexibility, renewable energy, and distributed energy resources.
if data centers limited load a mere 0.5 percent (less than 44 hours out of the year), the grid could handle 98 GW of new load---enough to power 70 million homes.

letters.org: CHAMBER OF COMMERCE OF THE UNITED STATES
letters.desc: The Chamber wants the process to encourage voluntary options such as demand response, storage, and hybrids when stakeholders accept them, and to preserve utility-specific and regional flexibility so working approaches are not disrupted.
quotes: the preexisting process, handled primarily on a state-level basis, is not broken everywhere. Many large loads have been and continue to be connected at the transmission level nationwide. Thus, any reforms proposed or implemented because of this proceeding should be mindful to not upend the progress that is currently being made to interconnect large loads across the country; new delays should not inadvertently be imposed by reforms intended to achieve the opposite result.

Support for Innovation: The interconnection process should encourage the adoption of innovative technologies and practices, such as expanded use of voluntary demand response programs, energy storage, hybrid facilities, and advanced grid management systems, provided that such options are amenable to all directly impacted entities, to optimize the integration of large loads.

flexibility should be provided – consistent with the final paragraph of the ANOPR – to ensure that equivalent or superior solutions to large load interconnection can be continued or newly developed on a utility-specific or larger regional bases, as appropriate.

letters.desc: CEBA supports interconnection designs that enable large load flexibility but opposes mandates. Most data center workloads are mission-critical and cannot be curtailed; any flexibility incentives must be structured as voluntary pathways to allow innovation without forcing operational risks on customers.
quotes: it is essential that interconnection design for large loads is structured to enable innovation and competition through voluntary pathways rather than mandates.

letters.desc: ClearPath argues that study assumptions and interconnection agreements must reflect the dispatchable nature of large loads such as thermal energy storage, electrolyzers, and electric arc furnaces. Worst-case study assumptions impose unnecessary upgrade costs on flexible loads, and interconnection agreements must not bar these loads from providing ancillary services or wholesale market participation.
quotes: ClearPath recommends that FERC require transmission providers to study large loads based on their known operating characteristics to increase the accuracy of these studies, avoid unnecessary network upgrades that can slow interconnection, and reduce excessive costs.

We recommend that FERC adopt a similar approach for studying large load withdrawals and/or injections. This advances just and reasonable rates by avoiding overestimation of the impacts of large loads through study assumptions that depict worst-case scenarios, such as curtailable large loads withdrawing at full capacity during peak demand periods

Any interconnection agreement for large load cannot prohibit the load from engaging in jurisdictional wholesale market activities such as the provision of energy (e.g., discharge of energy from storage into the grid) or ancillary services, including voltage support and other similar support for balancing the grid.
FERC must ensure that dispatchable large loads, in addition to co-located generating facilities, are fully compensated for providing energy and ancillary services to the grid.

Cost-allocation of network upgrades that combine volumetric and coincident peak demand charges can incentivize flexible large loads to avoid system peaks, therefore reducing system impacts and the need for additional infrastructure investments.
This regulatory framework incentivized EAFs to curtail load during critical peak demand and shift production, leading to a reduction of peak loads by 91%.

letters.desc: AI-SCA urges FERC to require transmission providers to build flexibility into large load interconnection procedures so they can accommodate the diverse supply arrangements and load types seeking connection.
quotes: we urge the Commission to encourage additional parameters and information from transmission providers to develop large load interconnection procedures that provide flexibility and that result in interconnection times that are faster than current processes.

letters.desc: Committee supports offering large loads non-firm, curtailable service in exchange for expedited grid connection, as this allows substantial demand to be served without constructing new transmission or generation facilities.
quotes: FERC should require transmission providers to offer non-firm, curtailable service in exchange for a large load interconnection applicant being given an expedited pathway to connect to the grid.

Allowing large loads to take flexible service and taking a 'connect and manage' type approach to interested customers could allow the grid to serve a substantial amount of demand without needing to construct new transmission or generation facilities.

letters.desc: Constellation supports allowing curtailable large loads to begin service under interruptible transmission service rather than waiting for full firm upgrade completion. It cites Duke University research showing modest curtailment rates can unlock tens of GW of new load integration without new capacity.
quotes: While expediting the interconnection studies of flexible load is a good step, the Commission should endorse other paths that would allow curtailable large loads and dispatchable hybrid resources to connect without first requiring the completion of system upgrades needed to support firm transmission service at peak, and without requiring any additional capacity.

letters.desc: Constellation proposes operational flexibility mechanisms for LCEP to handle load reduction or outage events, mirroring surplus and hybrid interconnection protections, so that no-net-injection conditions are always met.
quotes: The new generation must be "commensurate with the new load" and "deliverable" only to the new load with which it is paired—no net injections onto the grid beyond the existing generator's rights would be allowed.

letters.desc: CEA supports reforms to improve and expedite siting of energy infrastructure, including electric and gas transmission, generation, and large-load interconnection.
quotes: CEA enthusiastically supports reforms that improve and expedite the siting of energy infrastructure – whether it be electric and gas transmission, electric generation or large-load interconnection.

letters.desc: Critical Loop strongly supports creating a tariff-backed Large-Load Flexibility Commitment that credits curtailment-ready loads and co-located storage. The filer argues existing technology makes large loads technically flexible today, and that pairing enforceable limits with time-varying operating envelopes and real-time telemetry unlocks faster connections. Capacity market recognition and BESS bridge operation are companion elements.
quotes: Establish a Large‑Load Flexibility Commitment (LLFC) in the pro forma tariff; an opt‑in construct under which a load accepts specified curtailment and/or relies on on‑site or adjacent supply under defined conditions and require transmission providers to model LLFC parameters explicitly in interconnection studies

transmission providers should evaluate interconnections against those limits with explicit non‑performance contingencies rather than defaulting to a static, all‑resources‑unavailable maximum‑withdrawal assumption that obscures the value of on‑site batteries

the transmission provider should issue time‑varying operating envelopes that cap a site's net withdrawals (and, if applicable, net injections). The customer's certified control system must enforce the envelope autonomously and provide real‑time telemetry confirming compliance

Systematize and automate flexible interconnections by requiring publication of hosting‑capacity‑style data for load (hourly and seasonal headroom, constraints, expected curtailment windows) and by offering standardized flexible options (limited‑load profiles, non‑firm service, and joint‑study paths for hybrid or adjacent resources)
RTOs/ISOs should recognize LLFCs in capacity accreditation or allow appropriate adjustments to procurement obligations when loads accept enforceable limits and provide verifiable response

Recognize BESS‑enabled bridge operation as a low‑impact path that can permit faster than new combustion generation, improves power quality and ride‑through for large loads, and buys time while export or transmission upgrades for new generation proceed
Speed‑to‑power is a core reliability metric for U.S. industry and AI infrastructure; policy should meet the moment

letters.desc: Critical Loop supports an opt-in Large-Load Flexibility Commitment framework under which large loads can interconnect faster by committing to enforceable operating envelopes backed by on-site or adjacent resources. Curtailment obligations should be expressed in duration, magnitude, or frequency using probabilistic modeling. Studies must model these envelopes explicitly rather than defaulting to static maximum-withdrawal assumptions.
quotes: Critical Loop proposed a Large-Load Flexibility Commitment ("LLFC") construct that would allow large loads to interconnect faster when they commit to enforceable operating envelopes supported by on-site or adjacent resources, backed by telemetry, verification, and non-performance provisions.

An LLFC-style flexible connection can address the transmission bottleneck by defining a mix of firm and conditional service within an operating envelope, while complementary "bring your own capacity" mechanisms can address the generation bottleneck by ensuring that the firm portion of the load is backed by accredited capacity paid for by the customer.
when a large load accepts a flexible connection and procures or brings capacity sufficient to meet its firm service, it is effectively internalizing much of the marginal cost of its interconnection.

Requirements to curtail should be expressed in duration, magnitude, or frequency and should be built from time-series and probabilistic tools rather than relying only on worst-case deterministic assumptions.

we ask the Commission to ensure that flexible solutions and LLFCs are studied on a basis that can be compared with traditional upgrades. This occurs by requiring transmission providers to explicitly model enforceable flexibility and operating envelopes, rather than defaulting to static maximum-withdrawal assumptions that treat all co-located resources as absent or charging.

letters.desc: Crusoe supports flexible load incentives but insists that eligibility for expedited treatment should require demonstrated curtailment capability, not just qualitative commitments.
quotes: streamlined processes should prioritize large facilities above 100 MW.  For example, Crusoe has under development facilities in the 1,200 MW range with both grid interconnection and onsite natural gas production.

The Commission should instead establish clear, objective criteria that require interconnection customers to demonstrate both technical capability and financial commitment beyond mere qualitative assurances of curtailment flexibility.

it is critical that companies must demonstrate actual technical ability to curtail loads and advance flexible computing to be eligible for expedited interconnection.  If there are no stringent requirements for flexible load, the Commission could inadvertently create inefficiencies if unproven technologies are prioritized and expedited.

letters.desc: DCC supports expedited study for flexible or paired configurations but argues the pathway should not exclude non-curtailable loads, since coordination of new load and incremental generation alone justifies expedited treatment.
quotes: Support exists for creating expedited pathways for configurations that provide demonstrable grid benefits, with many commenters emphasizing the need for such pathways to accommodate the diverse operational profiles of large loads.

expedited processes should not be limited to curtailable loads, as this may be incompatible with operational requirements, and that coordination of new load and incremental generation alone warrants expedited study.

letters.desc: Data center heat reuse is a proven technology that can reduce electricity demand by 10 to 30 percent, avoiding construction of dozens of large power plants. Energy efficiency should be part of FERC's solution set, and FERC should incentivize reductions through speed-to-power benefits in the interconnection process rather than market payments, since permanent reductions are more valuable than flexible demand response.
quotes: data centers—the largest individual sources of projected load growth—can reduce their facilities electricity demand by 10 to 30% by reusing their waste heat

Such energy efficiency tools provide several benefits that are directly related to the issues raised in this docket, including tempering wholesale rates and facilitating speed-to-power by making efficient use of headroom on the system
energy efficiency solutions can have a direct and measurable impact on data center demand and should be considered as part of FERC's solution set

Because cooling operations can account for 40% of data center electricity consumption, these facilities can mitigate their overall electricity needs by reusing the data center's heat in other applications

Data center heat reuse can reduce data center electricity demand by 10 to 30%, which translates to "reduc[ing] new power demand by as much as 27 GW, [and] avoiding the construction of as many as 54 new conventional 500 megawatt (MW) power plants."
data center heat reuse is a proven technology that has been widely adopted across Europe, it remains an underutilized tool in the United States
While demand reductions can play a key role in resolving resource constraints there is little incentive for data centers to implement these actions unilaterally
FERC has a unique role and opportunity to incentivize demand reductions, and it should use this power to protect existing customers

DGA recommends that such incentives should focus on speed to power rather than market payments for two main reasons. First, unlike traditional demand response and load flexibility tools, which provide real time flexibility to the energy markets, proactive demand reductions provide permanent reductions. Second, time is money and there is more leverage in providing an incentive to interconnect quicker (whether through a new load interconnection process or via the generation interconnection process) than there is in potential future market payments

letters.desc: DEC argues that flexible digital infrastructure loads, including bitcoin miners and data centers, already provide real-time curtailment and reliability support. It wants FERC to formally recognize this flexibility in interconnection procedures, OATT frameworks, and cost rules, and to create a voluntary expedited track for customers that commit to verifiable curtailment agreements.
quotes: Bitcoin miners have already proven that large electrical loads can act as controllable, grid-responsive resources. Across multiple markets, mining facilities have curtailed load within seconds during periods of peak demand, providing measurable reliability support while maintaining stable operations.
These examples demonstrate that flexible load is already operating as a system asset, not a theoretical concept.

DEC supports the Department's initiative and encourages the Commission to establish a transparent, performance-based framework that recognizes flexibility as a grid resource, accelerates access to transmission, and ensures reliability and fairness for all users.

The Commission should direct jurisdictional transmission providers to include clear procedures within their Open Access Transmission Tariffs (OATTs) for evaluating large, transmission-level customers capable of providing real-time telemetry and verifiable curtailment.
Recognizing flexible demand within existing OATT frameworks would not create new service categories but would clarify how transmission providers study, model, and coordinate with these facilities.
The Commission should direct transmission providers to establish a voluntary, incentive-based fast-track process for customers that commit to verifiable flexibility agreements.

The Commission should affirm DOE's principle that large loads and hybrid facilities remain responsible for their assigned upgrade costs but clarify that those demonstrating verifiable curtailment or on-site generation may qualify for phased or partial cost responsibility.

The Commission should leverage its existing technical conference and regional stakeholder processes along with its existing partnerships with the National Association of Regulatory Utility Commissioners (NARUC) to evaluate how flexible large loads can better participate in reliability and market operations.

letters.desc: DPN calls FERC support for integrating flexible loads critical and pushes for non-firm withdrawal rights, expedited study for curtailable facilities, and clear non-firm load pathways. Flexibility is the core value it wants the rule to reward.
quotes: FERC’s support for expediting the integration of flexible loads is critical to bolster the nation’s power systems.
FERC should also require that flexible loads have non-firm withdrawal rights, ensuring that excess load on the grid can be monetized during period of low demand
the interconnection study of large loads that agree to be curtailable and hybrid facilities that agree to be curtailable and dispatchable should be expedited.
NERC should have a flexible load category. Reliability standards should emphasize grid resilience on the supply side and be transparent, achievable, market-based solutions on the demand side.
There must be a clear pathway to interconnect non-firm, flexible large load- SPP is already considering a process called PALS so examples exists.

letters.desc: Duke Energy supports flexibility for transmission providers to adapt study requirements as reliability knowledge evolves and to tailor Electric Service Agreements to individual large load characteristics. It also sees merit in conditional, time-limited service as a bridge solution.
quotes: the transmission provider must have the flexibility to quickly adjust its customer requirements to respond to newly identified risks and emergent needs.

Duke Energy recognizes that there may be opportunities to identify 'bridge' solutions for limited, temporary interconnection service rights without eliminating the need for full interconnection service studies that identify the need for long-term infrastructure expansion.

letters.desc: EDF argues that operational flexibility is the key differentiator among large loads. Curtailable and dispatchable loads can reduce congestion and provide demand response, so they should face lighter study requirements, lower charges, and faster interconnection timelines than inflexible loads.
quotes: the Commission should adopt a flexible, performance-based framework that (1) recognizes the diversity within the large load industries (e.g., AI, crypto mining, hydrogen, e-fuels, and carbon capture, utilization and storage (CCUS)); (2) encourages "grid-light" development structures, such as hybrid facilities that put minimal stress on the grid, and avoids inadvertently penalizing innovative co-located load configuration models; and (3) addresses much needed reforms to the Commission's Public Utility Holding Company Act (PUHCA) regulations to allow independent power producers, such as exempt wholesale generators (EWGs), to make direct sales to large loads (in states where it is allowed) without losing PUHCA exemptions for upstream owners.

A bifurcated or tiered review process should be implemented, allowing low-impact loads that are inherently less likely to cause significant transmission system upgrades to be studied and brought online more quickly than higher-impact loads.
Loads with considerable operating flexibility, such as crypto mining load, should not be treated the same as AI data centers that need "five-nines" power reliability.

The Commission should fast-track curtailable loads and curtailable/dispatchable hybrid facilities with firm expedited timelines.  Given that curtailable load and dispatchable generation at hybrid facilities can be beneficial and useful to day-to-day grid operations, interconnection timelines should be significantly reduced – in some cases to as little as 60 days.

Hybrid structures that are dispatchable and/or curtailable and place minimum demands on the transmission system (i.e., "grid-light") should pay less in grid costs than co-location structures where the load requires five-nines reliability.  Services provided by curtailable load should be eligible for demand response revenues.  This is required by the Commission's beneficiary pays principle.

letters.desc: EEI supports flexible interconnection approaches, including SPP's conditional transmission service for High Impact Large Load customers, as expedited mechanisms that utilities and RTOs can tailor to serve large loads quickly.
quotes: EEI shares the Administration's commitment to energy dominance and specifically supports improving the speed, efficiency, fairness, and predictability of large load interconnections.
A new SPP proposal to create conditional transmission service to integrate High Impact Large Load customers quickly.

letters.desc: EPSA agrees that load customers willing to commit to curtailability and dispatchability should receive expedited interconnection study treatment, consistent with the ANOPR's principle on flexible loads.
quotes: EPSA firmly agrees that, when a large load customer agrees to be curtailable and dispatchable in order to assist in system reliability and flexibility in defined circumstances, that load should be subject to an expedited interconnection study process.

letters.desc: ELCON supports flexibility in study processes for curtailable and dispatchable loads and calls for clear definitions to make those commitments enforceable. It also urges compensation mechanisms for the ancillary-service-like reliability value that flexible large loads provide, which would reduce the need for new transmission and generation.
quotes: ELCON appreciates the flexibility provided by principles five through seven to study load interconnection requests according to their operational needs and allow for expedited study for those customers agreeing to be curtailable and/or dispatchable.
the Commission should implement safeguards that clearly define "curtailable" and "dispatchable" including details of how much, when, and how in order to enforce those commitments.

the Commission should expand upon Principle 12 to actively encourage large loads to become system solutions. Curtailable and dispatchable large loads provide a demonstrable system benefit akin to essential ancillary services (such as operating and contingency reserves). The final rule must establish clear mechanisms to compensate these customers for the reliability value they provide, creating a critical financial incentive to offer flexible service that ultimately defers costly transmission and generation build-out for the benefit of all ratepayers.

letters.desc: ECA strongly supports clearing pathways for flexible near-term power arrangements, including co-location, bring-your-own-power, and behind-the-meter resources. These approaches shift costs to private investors rather than ratepayers. ECA also supports faster interconnection timelines for loads that agree to curtailment or flexibility.
quotes: leveraging opportunities for these quickly emerging large loads to utilize flexible arrangements to secure and pay for their own power supply—such as the hybrid (sometimes called "co-location") arrangements described by the Secretary in the ANOPR, "bring your own power" models, utilization of behind the meter generation and microgrids, and the like—is also essential to addressing threats to customer affordability and ensuring that private investors, not captive ratepayers, take on the costs and risks of rapid large load growth.

ECA suggests a guideline requiring that transmission providers have in place a large load interconnection process that, under normal circumstances, can be completed in two years, with an exception for large load customers that provide flexibility or take other steps to limit the need for infrastructure upgrades (which, consistent with the seventh principle in the ANOPR, should be significantly faster).

ECA strongly agrees that large load customers that agree to be flexible or provide curtailment that reduces the need for extensive network upgrades should receive the benefit of faster interconnection timelines.

the study requirements and parameters do not later inappropriately restrict the ability of large load customers with on-site resources to provide services back to the grid, individually or through aggregation.

letters.desc: ECA supports greater use of behind-the-meter generation aggregation under Order 2222, including in non-RTO regions, and endorses open season models that let customers fund infrastructure or utilize off-peak capacity. ECA views these as tools that can accelerate interconnection while benefiting system reliability and all customers.
quotes: ECA strongly supports comments emphasizing the value to all customers of greater aggregation and use of behind-the-meter generation resources.

Fully implementing aggregation models under Order No. 2222, and encouraging their adoption in non-RTO regions, is critical to taking advantage of these resources to the benefit of system reliability and all customers.

ECA supports further examination of the potential for open season models to allow customers to express interest in funding new infrastructure or flexibly utilizing off-peak capacity to meet their needs.

letters.desc: ECA supports giving large load customers direct opportunities to signal willingness to pay and contract for needed transmission capacity, through open seasons or other market-responsive approaches. This would address cost-shift concerns while preserving customer choice.
quotes: More opportunities for large load customers to directly signal their willingness to pay for needed transmission capacity and contract to do so, whether through open seasons or other innovative market-responsive approaches, would directly address concerns about cost shifts to existing customers.

letters.desc: Emerald AI strongly supports creating a dedicated FLFT that expedites interconnection for loads that commit to verifiable, software-defined flexibility. The filing argues the rule must adopt a technology-neutral, performance-based definition of curtailment so that software-orchestrated demand reduction counts as valid curtailment. It also recommends operator control be satisfied by a secure, auditable software interface rather than physical disconnection.
quotes: We are particularly supportive of Principle 7 and urge the Commission to create a "Flexible Load Fast Track" (FLFT) that rewards verifiable flexibility with what large loads value most: faster and larger interconnections for new facilities seeking swift access and existing facilities seeking larger and speedy capacity to upgrade to latest-generation computing technology.

The Commission should instead adopt a performance-based definition of flexibility, consistent with the shift toward performance-based standards seen in other areas of grid regulation. If a facility can demonstrate, through telemetry and secure software interfaces, that it will reduce its withdrawal from 100 MW to 75 MW within the required timeframe of a signal, it effectively provides the same reliability value as a physical breaker, but with vastly higher economic efficiency.
The final rule should be technology-neutral and performance-based, recognizing the full spectrum of on-site flexibility.
Emerald AI strongly recommends this be defined as a secure, standardized, and auditable software interface, not direct, physical utility control.

Annual Event Limits: Setting a reasonable ceiling on annual curtailment events prevents excessive dispatch and ensures that flexible loads are used strategically, during genuine system stress, rather than as routine operational tools. AI data centers and next-generation AI Factories engage in the most economically critical workloads of the entire economy, so their curtailment should be extremely judicious.

letters.desc: Emerald AI supports defining flexibility in performance-based, technology-neutral terms where any method to verifiably reduce net load qualifies, regardless of whether via software, hardware, or hybrid approaches. This includes recognizing software-defined flexibility as equivalent to generation for grid balancing.
quotes: We align ourselves with the broad coalition of commenters—including the Advanced Energy Management Alliance (AEMA), utilities, transmission owners, and technology companies—in supporting a Flexible Load Fast Track (FLFT).
harness the full suite of flexibility technologies in a technology-neutral and performance-based way.

If a facility can verifiably reduce its net load at the Point of Interconnection (POI) within a specified timeframe, the method used to achieve that reduction should be irrelevant to the transmission provider.
Emerald AI specifically urges the Commission to recognize Software-Defined Flexibility as a valid form of dispatchability and curtailment, equivalent to generation.
A reduction in demand (megawatts off) is physically equivalent to an increase in supply (megawatts on) for the purposes of balancing the system.

letters.desc: Enchanted Rock supports Commission policies that incentivize load flexibility as a primary tool to expedite interconnection, strengthen reliability, and manage grid congestion. Flexible loads paired with dispatchable generation can reduce peak demand assumptions in transmission planning, thereby reducing upgrade needs and accelerating timelines.
quotes: Enchanted Rock recommends that the Commission adopt policies to incorporate and incentivize load flexibility as a tool to expedite the interconnection of large loads, which in turn, will enhance grid reliability and help to ensure affordability for all classes of customers.
LCDG is a practical and effective solution that would mitigate transmission constraints and address growing electricity demand associated with the influx of large load facilities.

Under circumstances where transmission is unavailable, under LCDG, on-site generation assets would serve as prime power to the large load facility that are waiting for transmission upgrades to be built.

LCDG enables loads to operate as non-firm service customers, thus allowing facilities to be studied as integrated load-generation assets to manage near-term transmission constraints and supply chain bottlenecks.

LCDG offers dispatchable on-site generation that, under grid operator control, can be called on to reduce load or export back to the grid during peak periods, which strengthens reliability and manages grid congestion.

the Commission should consider making large load facilities paired with generation, or large load facilities willing to participate under non-firm service, eligible for an expedited interconnection process.

the Commission should direct the North American Electric Reliability Corporation ('NERC') to review and revise its standards to recognize the flexibility created by large loads deploying on-site or co-located generation as a standard operational and planning tool.

large loads can be made flexible with respect to the transmission system through the deployment of on-site or co-located generation. Acknowledging load flexibility during the transmission planning and interconnection processes allows transmission planners to assume lower peak demand for the associated load facility, thereby reducing the immediate need for transmission upgrades and expediting interconnection timelines.

letters.desc: Enchanted Rock argues load flexibility lets planners assume lower peak demand, reducing immediate upgrade needs and speeding interconnection. It endorses interruptible and temporary opt-in service as a bridge that lets large loads operate before transmission upgrades complete, and cites SPP's HILLGA and CHILLS as expedited-pathway models.
quotes: Acknowledging load flexibility during the transmission planning and interconnection processes allows transmission planners to assume lower peak demand for the associated load facility, thereby reducing the immediate need for transmission upgrades and expediting interconnection timelines.

a joint study process would allow LCDG and hybrid facilities to be studied based on their operational behavior and net load impacts, which Enchanted Rock believes will result in less strain on the transmission system, unlock available grid headroom, optimize existing transmission infrastructure and more accurately model the flexible capabilities of the system.
interruptible service can serve as a bridge to full service while transmission upgrades are completed.
a temporary flexibility option that large loads can opt into . . . therefore mitigate[ing] some . . . risks and allow[ing] for faster load interconnection.

Efforts such as Southwest Power Pool, Inc. (“SPP”)’s High Impact Large Load Generation Assessment (“HILLGA”) and anticipated Conditional High Impact Large Load Service (“CHILLS”) proposal are examples of proposals that will create expedited pathways for interconnecting large loads.

letters.desc: State demand response programs that run outside RTO visibility suppress wholesale prices, hiding true scarcity. ETI argues FERC must direct RTOs to account for these programs so that spot prices reflect actual system conditions, particularly as large loads add new demand.
quotes: Since these demand response programs are not integrated into the wholesale price formation process, the RTO-ISOs do not have visibility into the demand (load) that takes place in these areas.

Without explicit FERC direction, ISOs will simply continue to see state-sponsored demand response initiatives as missing load that suppresses prices even in circumstances where true system conditions dictate high spot prices, or even scarcity.

letters.org: Enerwise Global Technologies, LLC dba CPower
letters.desc: Load flexibility can be deployed more quickly than new generation, avoiding long construction timelines and interconnection delays. It provides immediate tools to balance supply and demand while generation assets are being built.
quotes: While new generation and transmission infrastructure will be part of the solution, other more quickly deployable solutions, such as load flexibility, will be necessary. Simply put, load flexibility helps balance supply and demand by reducing demand when called upon by the grid operator.

The ANOPR proposes to allow for expedited interconnection of large loads that co-locate with generation. While this is likely to be an important part of the solution space, relying on new generation alone to meet increased demand will put reliability at risk in the intervening years that it takes for these generation assets to come online.

Given this reality, load flexibility – a more readily available resource - must also play a part in enabling the interconnection of large loads. Leveraging load flexibility has a couple of key advantages: it will be quicker to deploy, and it will be less expensive in most cases.

Load flexibility can be deployed much more quickly than new generation because no interconnection process or lengthy construction period applies to load flexibility that uses an already installed behind the meter asset or does not use a behind the meter asset at all.

letters.desc: ENGIE consistently calls for flexibility in implementation: regions should set thresholds, protection systems should be technology-agnostic, expedited queue flexibility terms must be defined, and RTOs should be permitted to propose region-specific curtailment thresholds.
quotes: ENGIE emphasizes, however, that retaining flexibility is paramount. It will be essential that any new requirements take into account, and at times defer to regional differences and regional knowledge of system conditions.

ENGIE recommends that the Commission allow for flexibility in implementation of a given megawatt threshold by deferring to the regions in setting a reasonable threshold. The Commission should require that ISOs and RTOs conduct a transparent stakeholder process to determine an appropriate threshold while relying on relevant system and queue data.
hybrid facility owners should have the flexibility to install protection systems of their choice as long as they meet the requisite industry standards.

ENGIE supports the concept of expedited interconnection for these types of facilities where load brings its own generation and/or storage. ENGIE recommends that the Commission consider establishing a separate queue for this purpose.

If these requirements are left unparameterized a project will struggle with commercial feasibility. It is next to impossible for a facility to plan around the requirements and there is almost no way to finance facilities that are exposed to these types of undefined risks.

letters.desc: Entergy strongly supports regional flexibility and opposes any uniform national rule that does not account for differences among states and RTOs. MISO South's existing processes work well and should not be disrupted by blanket federal requirements.
quotes: We are concerned that a nationwide one-size fits all rule issued by the Commission could overstep State jurisdiction over retail service and disrupt effective State-level resource planning processes.

The Entergy Operating Companies believe our existing processes for the interconnection and service to large loads are working, as they balance new customer timelines with secure, reliable, and affordable service to all customers using existing regulatory frameworks.

it is important that the Commission avoid blanket rules that fail to account for such differences.  In particular, Entergy Services urges the Commission to avoid ordering any blanket rules that could interfere with retail jurisdictional resource planning that currently takes place in MISO South, as these processes are working well.
the Commission should allow individual utilities to submit proposals that specifically address the technical details involved in studying new loads or the requirement of operational limitations.

the Commission should eschew any formal or uniform federal queue requirement for loads.  A one-size-fits-all, Commission-regulated queue process has the potential to be inefficient, and fraught with litigation and conflict.

letters.desc: Entergy argues that demand response and curtailability are retail supply matters under state jurisdiction, not federal interconnection issues. FERC should not use a new load interconnection rule to override state decisions on reliable retail supply arrangements.
quotes: the Commission should not use a new load interconnection rule to substitute its judgment for that of state regulators about what constitutes reliable retail supply arrangements

letters.desc: The core of Eolian's filing is that enforceable flexibility commitments from curtailable loads and dispatchable hybrid facilities should be recognized in the interconnection process through queue priority and streamlined study. Without this, rising upgrade costs and resource adequacy burdens will persist. Permanent non-firm service pathways are essential to make flexibility commercially viable.
quotes: Eolian strongly supports the Commission's effort to ensure the timely and orderly interconnection of large loads to the transmission system.

Flexibility commitments from loads and hybrid resources can help to protect existing customers by avoiding the need for transmission system upgrades and allowing large loads to reduce the resource adequacy impacts of their interconnection and allow large loads—and the resources needed to serve them—to come online quickly without the need for extensive study or network upgrades.

recognizing enforceable commitments from large load customers and hybrid facilities to curtail and dispatch when called upon, providing transmission service and balancing authority operations protocols that match these commitments, and appropriately rewarding these commitments with preferred treatment in the interconnection process.

the Commission should direct transmission providers to provide for a FERC-jurisdictional load interconnection process that grants queue priority to loads that make commitments to curtail, and hybrid facilities that make commitments to dispatch and curtail, such that (a) the load or hybrid resource reduces the system's need for capacity or Network Resources, and/or (b) avoids the need for network upgrades.

the Commission should direct transmission providers to offer non-firm or conditional firm transmission service to hybrid resources that allow them to inject and withdraw up to their full potential, subject to specified system conditions and their flexibility commitments.
Without access to non-firm or conditional firm service, much of the economic value of the hybrid resource model will be lost.

serial streamlined study of load and hybrid facilities is possible where the facility nominates operating limits (in MW) for aggregate net injections and withdrawals of power, installs necessary control equipment to ensure that the facility is capable of following the dispatch controls of the transmission system operator and balancing authority and respecting operating limits at all times, and is capable at any time of complete self-supply or otherwise curtailing the load such that the facility can take transmission service on a non-firm basis.

failure to truly enable flexible loads and provide them a means to internalize the benefits they provide to the system could otherwise result in the worst of all worlds: shifting large load interconnection to a standardized federal process that slows down progress by disrupting the potential for state innovation and failing to reduce the monumental cost of transmission expansion and capacity growth otherwise necessary to integrate large loads into the transmission system.
the Commission should also require that transmission providers allow a pathway to permanent non-firm operation that does not require a subsequent service conversion.

letters.desc: Eolian argues that curtailability and dispatchability should be rewarded with faster interconnection, because flexible facilities cause fewer system impacts and can be safely integrated without triggering broader queue restudies. It supports non-firm transmission service as the operational framework that makes flexibility commitments meaningful.
quotes: Operating limits can be enforced through physical system protection and control equipment, through contractual and legal tariff obligations to obey dispatch instructions, and through FERC and NERC enforcement actions.

Taken together, these examples clearly demonstrate that operating limits on hybrid facilities' net injections and withdrawals to and from the grid can be safely enforced, and therefore assigned based on the amounts requested, and not necessarily their nameplate capabilities, in such cases where such requested injections and withdrawals are below the amount of nameplate generation and load respectively.

The establishment of a non-firm network transmission service tier should be a core part of any final rule, as such a service tier is integral to enabling transmission providers to expedite interconnection for curtailable large loads and curtailable and dispatchable hybrid facilities.

just as an express checkout line appropriately rewards those whose needs can be addressed more quickly with faster service, it is appropriate to study curtailable and dispatchable facilities on a separate, streamlined basis due to their lesser impacts on the broader system
adopting hybrid-specific rules are a consensus, no-regrets reform that allows the Commission to tackle the lowest hanging fruit of the large load growth challenge.

letters.desc: Eolian supports non-firm and curtailable transmission service options for loads that commit to limit withdrawals during grid constraints, whether co-located or merely adjacent to supply. It asks that such service be available during normal (non-emergency) conditions and be offered on a permanent rather than time-limited basis.
quotes: we have not encountered any transmission provider that currently has a process which (i) adequately integrates or coordinates the interconnection of supply resources and load, (ii) provides developers of supply resources such as Eolian with adequate incentive to locate generation and storage assets in a manner that opens additional system headroom for load interconnection, or (iii) offers the full range of transmission service options necessary to allow supply and load to coordinate to optimally use the existing system and reduce transmission infrastructure needs.

The lack of tariff provisions to afford all three elements results in unjust and unreasonable or unduly discriminatory rates by exacerbating the reliability and affordability impacts of large load growth, while impeding speed-to-power for new large loads.

The relevant interconnection process must provide a path for permanent interconnection service. Temporary frameworks that hinge on subsequent processing through a standard queue create commercial risks that are likely to inhibit widespread use of these interconnection pathways.

The Commission must require transmission providers to offer transmission services that match the ability of loads to use the capabilities of adjacent generation, including non-firm and reduced service options. Such service must allow the load to take service when the grid is unconstrained and the supply resource is not available (including when a battery resource is charging) while electing to curtail when the grid is constrained.

the Commission should explicitly direct transmission providers to make the non-firm services available to all loads willing and able to limit withdrawals from the transmission system rather than limiting availability only to co-located loads.

whatever non-firm transmission services that the Commission directs transmission providers to offer in this proceeding must be designed to allow for broad availability of non-firm service during non-emergency conditions and not only during associated generator outages.

letters.desc: Equinix supports allowing aggregated resource packages that include proximate third-party flexibility resources, not just generation or storage behind the large load's meter. Urban colocation facilities should be able to contract with surrounding commercial, industrial, or residential resources to satisfy flexibility requirements.
quotes: it is not clear to us why the flexibility that could clearly offer our energy system such great benefit must, or even should, be either incorporated into the large load itself or necessarily located behind the same interconnection.
artificially constraining flexibility options to the those produced by large load itself could clearly create uneconomic outcomes by as much as orders of magnitude

Those data centers located in dense metropolitan areas should be able to tap into the wealth of flexibility opportunities that surround them, creating a mutual benefit for those commercial, industrial or even residential users that could receive enhanced energy equipment or could easily absorb curtailment at a much lower economic and performance cost.
large load interconnection customers should be allowed to include what could be termed 'aggregated resource' proposals in their interconnection requests.

Providing that study frameworks accurately model and value the relevant operational characteristics of the proposed large load along with its aggregated flexibility resources, it is not clear to us why study queue prioritization or any other exogenous benefit is necessary or appropriate.

letters.desc: esVolta argues that BESS makes large loads curtailable and dispatchable, which are the attributes the reform principles use to justify expedited treatment. The filer asks FERC to formally link BESS-backed flexibility to the expedited interconnection pathway.
quotes: In esVolta's view, the Commission's large-load reforms present an important opportunity to recognize that BESS can directly mitigate these power quality concerns and thereby assist in facilitating the timely and orderly interconnection of large loads consistent with the principles of reform outlined in this proceeding.

When properly configured, BESS can be dispatched to smooth the net load seen by the transmission system, mitigating sudden spikes and drops in demand and thereby transforming a volatile large load into a more "grid-friendly" net profile.
BESS enables the large loads to be curtailable or flexible and should jointly be eligible for an expedited pathway to interconnection.

letters.desc: ETX recommends expedited interconnection pathways for projects that pass higher readiness thresholds or can limit transmission system impacts. It also urges flexible sizing amendments during the study process so hybrid and co-located projects can right-size around modeling circularities rather than locking in suboptimal capacities early.
quotes: The Load Interconnection Study Procedures should establish expedited pathways for more mature projects that pass greater readiness thresholds and for projects with flexible requirements or capabilities that can limit transmission system impacts.

The Load Interconnection Study Procedures should allow for flexible project sizing amendments based on study results that encourage efficient use of transmission resources, especially for Hybrid and/or co-located projects where parallel load and generation studies will create modeling circularities.

letters.desc: Eversource argues a strict one-size-fits-all interconnection process would impede rather than facilitate large-load interconnection and could cause more harm than the status quo. It urges sufficient flexibility to address varied load types, hybrid arrangements, and region-specific rules.
quotes: an overly prescriptive and restrictive final rule arising out of this proceeding could result in more harm than the status quo to prospective large load customers, interconnecting transmission owners, and the public generally.
implementing a strict, one-size-fits-all interconnection process will impede rather than facilitate the interconnection of these large loads.
the Commission should also ensure that any final rule provides sufficient flexibility to address the different needs of large-load customers.
Any final rule arising out of this proceeding must be flexible enough to accommodate different load types and their needs.

the final rule should also be flexible enough to encompass different “hybrid” load arrangements, including those co-located with generation seeking standby service, behind-the-meter generation with voluntary curtailment/isolation, and other arrangements that may be sought by customers.

The final rule should also be flexible enough to allow transmission providers to develop and address region-specific rules and concerns (such as termination of co-located generator interconnection rights).

letters.desc: Exelon supports flexible approaches including BYOG and hybrid structures that let large loads and their generators share interconnection points, as long as cost and reliability obligations are fully preserved.
quotes: Exelon supports generator interconnection reforms that recognize the value in 'bring your own generation' ('BYOG') approaches, in which generation dedicated to serve specific large load customers comes online with financial support and commitments from those customers.

letters.desc: Fervo supports recognizing that curtailability and dispatchability materially reduce system impacts; geothermal-based hybrids are particularly well suited to provide predictable, operator-controlled responses that improve system reliability.
quotes: Fervo supports the Commission's proposal to expedite interconnection studies for large loads and hybrid facilities that agree to be curtailable or dispatchable, as these operational flexibilities materially reduce system impacts and allow transmission providers to study such projects with greater confidence.

Geothermal-based hybrid projects are particularly well suited for this approach because they can provide highly predictable, operator-controlled responses that improve system reliability during peak or contingency events.

An expedited study process that recognizes the reliability value of curtailable or dispatchable hybrids would help accelerate deployment of clean firm resources while allowing transmission providers to prioritize projects that offer the greatest operational benefit.

letters.desc: FirstEnergy proposes additional design features to keep the expansion rate fair over time. The customer's contribution would be set on the higher of actual or a minimum contractual demand to prevent cost-shifting through underutilization, and expansion obligations would be reallocated annually as more customers connect to the same facilities so no single participant overpays.
quotes: the customer's transmission-rate contribution could be calculated based on the higher of actual demand or a minimum contractual-demand threshold, preventing cost-shifting through underutilization. Likewise, expansion-rate obligations could be reallocated annually as additional customers interconnect to the same facilities, reducing the cost burden borne by any individual participant over time.

letters.desc: Fluence urges FERC to ensure that large load flexibility commitments can be satisfied by storage resources physically or electrically adjacent to the load, so that BESS can serve as the flexibility mechanism enabling an expedited pathway.
quotes: BESS is uniquely positioned to make large loads curtailable and flexible.
Given these highly desired attributes, the interconnection of hybrid facilities that include BESS should be expedited.
The Commission should ensure that load commitments to flexibility can be met by resources physically and/or electrically adjacent to load.

letters.desc: The GPSC engages with prospective large load customers on load flexibility and rate design as part of its economic development work, treating flexibility as one tool to manage system impacts.
quotes: The GPSC is able to support this economic development through engagement with businesses looking to locate in Georgia to ensure that the size and types of resources, opportunities for load flexibility, and rate designs meet the desired specifications.

letters.desc: Google supports expedited study treatment for loads that voluntarily offer curtailability or demand response, but insists flexibility must remain an incentive rather than a condition of interconnection.
