Generation commitments should match the load's ramp and utilization schedule on a one-for-one basis.
quotes: To ensure that the generation is appropriately tailored to the new load, those commitments should match the load's ramp and utilization schedule on a one-for-one basis with accredited generation, verified load flexibility, or demand response capabilities.

As with the rules governing colocation or electrically proximate pairs of load and generation, and as in SPP's HILL/HILLGA proposal, any new rules governing the interconnection of curtailable load must take the form of an incentive, not a requirement.

letters.desc: Google supports creating an optional expedited interconnection pathway for loads willing to curtail during system stress. Research cited by Google shows that even a 0.25% annual curtailment rate could accommodate 76 GW of new load, and flexible connections in PJM could cut wait times by three to five years.
quotes: any expedited processes are technology neutral and do not arbitrarily favor loads paired with generation over those capable of providing equivalent relief through flexibility.

a load curtailment rate of just 0.25% annually would allow for the integration of 76 GW of new load—the equivalent of 10% of the nation's current aggregate peak demand—with minimal generation capacity expansion.

combining flexible grid connections with a "bring-your-own-capacity" framework in PJM could shorten interconnection wait times by three to five years and maintain grid power availability for over 99% of hours, while requiring on-site resource dispatch for only 40 to 70 hours annually.

Rules governing the interconnection and operation of curtailable loads must account for how large loads, including data centers, operate in practice. Such rules must encourage innovation without being so onerous and/or impractical that they discourage large loads from opting to operate flexibly when doing so could be beneficial for the load and the system.

letters.desc: GridCARE supports an optional expedited study pathway for large loads that can commit to verifiable flexibility. The company cites emerging regional frameworks at PJM, SPP, and ISO-NE as evidence that this approach is workable and encourages FERC to establish a national framework allowing regional customization.
quotes: flexibility, when defined in measurable and verifiable terms, can help accelerate interconnections, reduce restudy risks, provide near-term operational headroom, and maintain reliability.

PJM's Critical Issue Fast Path, SPP's High-Impact Large Load process, and ISO-NE's ongoing work on load characterization all demonstrate that regions are exploring ways to streamline studies, incorporate temporal and behavioral data, better align study processes with actual system operations, and improve coordination with utilities.

Systematically incorporating this flexibility ecosystem into planning and operations will unlock existing capacity on the grid, accelerate interconnections, and enable beneficial load growth to preserve customer affordability and fund new infrastructure investment.

letters.desc: GridStor argues that batteries are inherently flexible and curtailable, enabling demand management for data centers and helping large loads meet ride-through and curtailment requirements. It wants reforms for flexible loads to recognize and extend to ESRs.
quotes: Energy Storage Resources (ESRs) are critical to helping get large loads online faster and reliably.
Batteries enable flexible demand management for data centers to ensure business continuity while complying with such requirements.

To the extent that the Commission seeks to develop rules to expedite transmission service studies of large loads that are flexible and curtailable, we respectfully request that such rules also enable speedy and timely transmission service studies of ESR charging.
It is also worth exploring whether RTOs/ISOs might offer different forms of transmission service to support such flexible and curtailable loads.

Other large loads and ESRs would benefit from a “conditional firm” transmission service, where pre-defined conditions (e.g., EEA, conservative operations, etc) require curtailment but where transmission service is otherwise expected—an improvement from as-available service that has little predictability.

letters.desc: Helion emphasizes that modern grids need generation capable of rapid ramping and precise coordination with load fluctuations. Helion's fusion technology is characterized as providing baseload power with dispatchability to respond within seconds, and the filing argues collocated generation enables true load flexibility and grid support.
quotes: Helion's fusion plants will deliver baseload power that is not fuel-limited with rapid dispatchability—ramping output dynamically in response to grid conditions within seconds through our inherent pulsed power system.

Calling data centers "flexible" does not mean they can simply absorb sudden cuts in power; real flexibility comes from collocated generation that can ramp up and down with their needs and support the grid in the process.

letters.desc: Heron asks the Commission to distinguish loads with integrated ride-through and load-smoothing, and to extend the expedited treatment being considered for flexible and curtailable loads to grid-forming loads.
quotes: The Commission's evolving reliability framework should distinguish between data centers designed with integrated ride-through and load-smoothing capability and those without.
The expedited study pathway the Commission is considering for flexible and curtailable loads is a natural starting point; grid-forming loads should qualify for comparable treatment.

letters.desc: System-wide demand reduction creates downward pressure on wholesale prices, benefiting all market participants. Commercial buildings with black rubber roofs are the most cost-effective near-term targets.
quotes: In the larger market, significant demand reduction will create downward pressure on electric wholesale prices, which will benefit everyone, including the large users like the data centers. In the end, everyone wins.
The low-hanging fruit for demand reduction lies with flat-roofed commercial buildings, most of which have a roofing system of black rubber.

letters.desc: The filer argues that data centers hold significant latent flexibility through workload shifting, UPS response, and on-site generation, and that current rules ignore this. She supports modernizing market participation rules so these capabilities reduce upgrade costs and system stress.
quotes: Modern data centers possess significant latent flexibility through workload shifting, UPS-based frequency response, and hybrid on-site generation.
Current interconnection rules treat these loads as static and inflexible, ignoring capabilities that could significantly reduce system stress and upgrade costs.

The Commission should establish a federal framework that lowers barriers to flexible resources, modernizes market participation rules for technologies like thermal energy storage (TES), and reforms cost allocation to reflect marginal impacts.

letters.desc: Kiesling argues that modern data centers and hyper-flexible loads such as thermal energy storage possess latent flexibility across multiple time scales that current rules ignore. She supports interconnection and market rules that recognize and reward this flexibility, citing research showing that modest curtailment commitments could integrate tens of gigawatts of new load on existing capacity.
quotes: Current interconnection rules treat these loads as static and inflexible, ignoring capabilities that could significantly reduce system stress and upgrade costs.

Norris et al. (2025) quantifies this potential: it finds that, with modest curtailment of just 0.25 %–0.5 % of annual uptime, U.S. balancing authorities could integrate nearly 76 GW–98 GW of new large loads using existing capacity without disruptive grid upgrades.
Hyper flexible loads like TES are being installed now with the operational capability and business model incentive to make robust, enforceable and dependable flexibility commitments.
The expedited queue access proposal is one step in the direction of valuing flexibility as a capability.
Aligning cost allocation with marginal impacts ensures that flexible loads remain part of the bulk system rather than retreating into private microgrids.

letters.desc: The commenter recommends that system operators have clear authority to mandate curtailment of large loads in emergencies and that curtailment priority relative to other resources be specified.
quotes: Recommend the possibility that curtailment may be mandatory at the system operator's instruction (for emergency situations) and request clarity on how curtailment priority will be established relative to other resources.

letters.desc: The filer supports requiring transmission planning to model large loads even when they offer to take non-firm service, because the regulatory framework does not currently accommodate non-firm planning and inflexible operating behavior creates cascading risk regardless of contractual flexibility.
quotes: Inflexible large loads have been demonstrated to reduce the Bulk Electric Systems (BES) ability to withstand disturbances, increasing risks of cascading outages during extreme events

Explore the need for augmentation of the TPL-001-5.1 to require explicit modeling of large, concentrated loads in both near term and long term planning assessments even if those projects are offering to take non-firm 'flexible' electric service.

offering non-firm transmission service may not meet the requirements in TPL-001. Under the current requirements, it is not permitted to plan the transmission system to provide electric service under TPL-001-5.1 on a non-firm basis (i.e., permitting non-consequential load loss).

letters.desc: Flexible and curtailable large loads should be evaluated using consequence-aware analytics that quantify, for specific grid locations and system states, the reliability value their flexibility provides. This enables expedited treatment based on measurable principles rather than categorical rules.
quotes: Flexible and curtailable large loads should be evaluated using real-time, consequence-aware analytics, which can quantify the reliability value of their flexibility and support the faster study track the ANOPR contemplates.
Consequence-aware analytics can quantify, for a specific location and system state, the headroom that a curtailable load frees up and the reliability margin its flexibility preserves.
The need to integrate large loads, including AI data centers, in a timely and orderly manner is urgent, and tools to do so reliably are largely available today.

letters.org: Industrial Energy Consumers of America et al.
letters.desc: The filers' XL Connect proposal requires large loads using the optional fast-lane process to demonstrate flexibility commitments, including curtailable load, behind-the-meter generation, or bring-your-own-generation arrangements, as a condition of eligibility.
quotes: the Industrial Customer Organizations respectfully propose that the Commission consider developing an elective, "fast-lane" interconnection approach that addresses regional transmission and resource adequacy impacts without cutting out the distribution utility or violating state-level tariffs.

letters.desc: iMasons supports faster interconnection for loads that voluntarily accept curtailment or dispatch, while protecting parties already in existing queues from disruption.
quotes: iMasons supports a final rule that accelerates the interconnection of large loads that voluntarily agree to be curtailable and dispatchable (i.e., flexible), provided that existing interconnection queues are not unduly and unjustly disrupted.

letters.desc: IFP calls Principle 7 the single most powerful near-term proposal. Expedited interconnection for curtailable loads can unlock 76 GW or more of new capacity with minimal grid expansion, bridging the gap between immediate AI demand and longer-horizon generation and transmission buildout.
quotes: IFP strongly supports the Principles identified in the Commission's ANOPR.

the ANOPR's principles directed at accelerating and standardizing large load interconnection are needed to maintain United States leadership in both AI research and development as well as AI deployment.
The most powerful proposal for immediate impact is Principle 7, which proposes that 'the interconnection study of large loads that agree to be curtailable... should be expedited.'
the US grid could integrate "76 GW of new load" with minimal expansion of the existing power system.
Adherence to these new, robust security standards should be a non-negotiable precondition for any large load to receive the 'speed-to-power' benefits (Principle 7) proposed in this ANOPR.

letters.desc: IECA supports developing Commission policy guidelines for controllable dispatch applied to Data Centers and co-located generators, enabling real-time coordination with grid operators during outage events.
quotes: We support the use of "Controllable Dispatch" and other technological means of managing outages or derates of either a Data Center or its associated generation facility. Commission consideration in this or another proceeding of policy guidelines for applications of "Controllable Dispatch" to Data Centers and co-located generation facilities could be beneficial.

letters.org: Invenergy Wind Development North America LLCInvenergy Solar Development North America LLCInvenergy Thermal Development Holdings LLC ,
letters.desc: Invenergy supports building in flexibility during the transition period, including an expedited track for loads with generator contracts, so that projects already prepared to move forward are not held up by the development of broader rules.
quotes: the Commission could issue rules creating an expedited interconnection process for load that has contracted with a generator.

letters.desc: The ANOPR framework should provide large customers enhanced flexibility for interstate transmission grid interconnection under federal oversight.
quotes: The proposed ANOPR lays out a framework that, if implemented, would provide Iron Mountain and other similarly situated customers enhanced flexibility when interconnecting to the interstate transmission grid.

letters.desc: ISO-NE favors qualifying curtailable large loads through wholesale market programs such as demand response, rather than manual out-of-market curtailment protocols. This supports expedited study eligibility while keeping operations orderly.
quotes: In order to accomplish an expedited large load study process for curtailable large loads, the terms and conditions related to when load is curtailed should be simple and clear as they will inform the study methodology.  An expedited large load study should be available only if the load is fully curtailable.

letters.desc: ITC supports the Secretary of Energy's effort to expedite and streamline large load interconnections as a path to efficient and transparent interconnection processes.
quotes: ITC generally supports Secretary of Energy Wright's effort to expedite and streamline the interconnection of large loads to the transmission system.

letters.desc: ITC contends that LRTP projects not subject to Order 1000 competitive solicitation allowed rapid development timelines critical for large load accommodation. The filer argues that subjecting these projects to solicitation would have added two years of delay, undermining in-service requirements and slowing data center interconnection.
quotes: current regulatory frameworks, including large loads' obligations to pay for the ongoing development, maintenance, and operation of the overall transmission system through network transmission service charges, accomplish these goals when paired with proactive transmission planning, the knowledge of local Transmission Owners, and other policies that promote optimal long-term solutions over quick or narrowly focused fixes.

ITC Midwest's forward-looking, proactive approach to grid development, reinforced through MISO's Long-Range Transmission Planning ("LRTP") portfolios, has enabled faster large-load interconnections by providing available regional capacity and reducing the scope and cost of network upgrades, benefiting both new customers and existing ratepayers.

A key factor in accommodating the data center growth in Iowa was ITC Midwest's ability to start developing the LRTP projects right after MISO Board approval due to the segments not being eligible for Order No. 1000 competition. If the projects had been subject to the solicitation process, it would have added almost two years of delay before determining who was responsible for construction, irreparably undermining the in-service timeline requirements.

letters.desc: The Alliance recommends that FERC require new large loads to curtail power during peak grid emergencies until they add enough generation to cover their own demand. Demand flexibility lets new loads interconnect quickly using existing grid headroom without new transmission.
quotes: FERC should require any new large load facility to reduce power use during peak load grid emergencies until that user has added enough generation capacity to cover its own energy demand.

letters.desc: LPPC highlights bring-your-own-power arrangements that require large load customers to procure or contract for their own generation, insulating other customers from capacity cost impacts.
quotes: Requires large load customers to procure or contract for their own generation supply.

letters.desc: Community Choice Aggregations are well-positioned to deliver flexible resources by integrating hybrid storage and generation assets with coordinated load programs. Flexibility should be incentivized as a competitive product available beyond utility-run programs, not by expediting interconnection timelines.
quotes: Data centers that co-locate storage or generating assets and have the ability to shift load in response to market or grid operating condition signals may be well-positioned to work with their local CCA to integrate their hybrid resources into a flexible load program that can benefit not only the data center as a customer, but all customers served by the CCA, by reducing peak demand through automated load reduction.
these flexibilities can and should be incentivized in ways other than faster interconnection.
Flexibility can be considered a competitive product, and should be available beyond defaulting to utility-run programs.

letters.desc: LIPA opposes uniform national ride-through and frequency standards as short-sighted and grid-risky, insisting transmission owners must adapt requirements to their own system topology. One-size-fits-all rules either become too permissive (compromising security) or too restrictive (making loads economically infeasible).
quotes: a one-size-fits-all standard for such measures is short-sighted and increases risk to the grid. Transmission owners and operators must have the flexibility to adapt and adopt prevention and mitigation measures within their interconnection procedures and standards, reflective of their own system's topology.

Accordingly, frequency and protection measures as well as ride-through standards for large loads cannot be a static, universal standard or study metric. Rather, the transmission owner and operators must have the ability to adapt these standards in a manner that provides an optimal balance of the objectives across all load facilities within its interconnected grid.
the Commission should ensure that any forthcoming rule provides for regional flexibility on ride through standards in order to meet the needs of a particular system.

If a large load facility is susceptible to rapid disconnection or load change in response to a system disturbance, then the large load interconnection study process should assess the potential system impact resulting from such abrupt changes; and As part of the planning, design and construction of interconnection facilities for large loads, transmission owners should have the right to require load to implement and maintain disturbance ride through capability that is necessary to ensure system stability and security.

letters.org: Louisiana Public Service CommissionMississippi Public Service Commission
letters.desc: The commissions support a flexible approach that accommodates regional differences and does not override state processes that are already working. They ask that any rule apply only where delays have been demonstrated and that states retain the ability to manage interconnections under their own successful procedures.
quotes: the rule should not apply to any transmission owner or transmission provider in the absence of a demonstration that large load interconnections are being met with significant delays

Even if the FERC technically is granted jurisdiction over large load interconnections to the interstate transmission system, it should refrain from exercising that jurisdiction in locations where it is not needed under principles of cooperative federalism.

any rules adopted should not be a one-size-fits-all proposition. Rules must take into account regional differences. State and RTO processes that have worked well should be accommodated and not changed. Flexibility is crucial to meeting the needs of new large loads and of the affected states.

letters.desc: LS Power supports integrating demand response frameworks into large-load interconnection agreements for flexible loads. Curtailment rights for hybrid facilities must be bounded by generation-load balance constraints, and resource adequacy planning must reflect curtailable load so that flexibility does not distort competitive price signals.
quotes: Large load interconnection rules should provide an expedited process for generation paired with co-located new large load. In order to qualify for expedited interconnection consideration, the large load must bring generation that matches its maximum capacity and energy needs.

Hybrid facilities interconnecting on an expedited basis (deferred transmission upgrades) can be fully curtailable. If associated generation is not providing sufficient energy for its load, then the load cannot look to the grid for its energy and if load is less than the generation supply, the generation may not come onto the grid (other than emergency dispatch).

it is also critical that the relevant regional energy markets send the appropriate price signal to indicate scarcity of supply resources such that the curtailment of flexible large loads cannot be used to undermine competitive energy market pricing by failing to reflect curtailable load in resource adequacy planning.

letters.org: Maine Office of the Public Advocate
letters.desc: Maine OPA supports incentivizing large loads to participate in curtailment, load flexibility, and demand response mechanisms as a way to minimize their impact on transmission rates and wholesale prices.
quotes: the Maine OPA also supports the recommendation to allow and/or incentivize large load customers to participate in curtailment, load flexibility, and other demand response mechanisms.

Such mechanisms allow these new large loads to minimize their impact on both transmission rates and wholesale market prices, as well as to reduce the cost of interconnection and the ongoing cost of electricity to these customers.

letters.org: Massachusetts Office of the Attorney General
letters.desc: The State Entities support ANOPR language encouraging curtailability and dispatchability for large loads, arguing that demand response and load flexibility reduce peak demand strain and the size of costly transmission upgrades. They urge FERC to consider expanding the rulemaking to capture additional flexibility mechanisms.
quotes: the State Entities support efforts by the Commission to protect ratepayers by allowing and/or incentivizing large load customers to participate in curtailment, load flexibility, and other demand response mechanisms.
the Commission should consider expanding the scope of this rulemaking to consider additional load flexibility mechanisms which can similarly alleviate the peak demand burden on ratepayers.

letters.desc: Meta opposes curtailment requirements as conditions for expedited treatment, arguing that data center operational requirements typically allow little downtime and that backup generation has regulatory constraints limiting its use for non-emergency demand response.
quotes: utilities should not limit expedited processes to only large loads or hybrid facilities 'that agree to be curtailable', which is discussed in paragraph 24 of the ANOPR. This limitation would be incompatible with the operational requirements of many data centers, which often allow for little downtime over the course of the year

letters.desc: Microsoft supports frameworks for voluntarily curtailable loads as a tool to accelerate AI infrastructure, while noting most data centers today have limited curtailment capability. It asks regulators and grid operators to work with data-center operators to define clear program parameters such as maximum curtailment times, frequency, and size.
quotes: Microsoft agrees that regulatory frameworks that allow for voluntarily curtailable loads make sense and will be an important tool for accelerating the deployment of critical AI infrastructure.
As discussed briefly below, most data centers today have limited curtailment capability.

Microsoft believes an expedited study process for curtailable loads and dispatchable hybrid facilities would be appropriate and consistent with the interests of the administration, so long as these arrangements do not create operational reliability risks and do not interfere with the interconnection of critical nonflexible large loads.

Microsoft encourages regulators, utilities, and grid operators—with consultation from datacenter operators—to create program clarity by identifying the type of flexibility that would bring value to the electric system and developing program parameters (such as maximum load curtailment times, frequency, and size) that are critical for datacenters to consider when making decisions about program participation.

letters.desc: MISO supports preserving regional flexibility by asking the Commission to let RTOs continue their own processes, or at most issue a policy statement rather than a binding rule. If a rule is unavoidable, MISO asks that the Independent Entity Variation be extended to allow significant regional deviations.
quotes: the Commission should be mindful of regional differences that might limit the success of a "one size fits all" mandate.  Shifting to standardized large load interconnection procedures could nullify currently effective processes and/or delay significant work that has been undertaken and currently ongoing.
shifting to a one-size-fits all approach could introduce delays to interconnecting large loads, which would be contrary to the very progress desired by the DOE and the Commission.

In lieu of requiring standard large load interconnection procedures, and in light of the concerns expressed above, the Commission should allow MISO, as well as other industry participants, to continue focusing attention on efficiently interconnecting large loads pursuant to processes that reflect the unique circumstances of their members, states, stakeholders, and transmission systems.

Alternatively, the Commission could refine the principles started by DOE and issue a policy statement to guide the industry processes to be used for large load interconnections.  This would enable Transmission Providers to craft unique solutions suited for their regions guided by Commission principles.

To the extent the Commission believes it must pursue standard large load interconnection procedures or another rule mandate through a formal rulemaking process, it should extend the "Independent Entity Variation" principle to any final rule.

letters.desc: The filing's through-line is that regional providers should retain the flexibility to craft solutions suited to their markets, technologies, and state regulatory contexts. The MISO Transmission Owners point to their own track record as evidence that regional approaches work.
quotes: the MISO Transmission Owners strongly encourage the Commission to refrain from taking generic action to develop a one-size-fits-all approach and instead, support transmission owners and transmission providers in their pursuit of solutions that facilitate the expeditious integration of large loads in a manner that preserves reliability and affordability.

Should the Commission elect to pursue the reforms proposed in the ANOPR, the MISO Transmission Owners recommend that the Commission provide transmission providers and their stakeholders significant flexibility in defining large loads, as they have the technical experience and judgment to appropriately and reasonably weigh operational, reliability, and administrative factors that are critical to defining large loads.

letters.desc: Given the tight April 2026 deadline and rapidly evolving technology, Missouri PSC urges FERC to adopt broad principles that allow regional innovation rather than prescriptive rules that cannot adapt to new circumstances.
quotes: The Secretary's abbreviated deadline of April 2026 for a final rule, combined with the novel legal and policy issues and rapidly evolving technology involved in large load interconnections, should warrant a cautious approach. FERC should consider adopting broad principles that allow for innovation and regional flexibility, rather than narrow prescriptions.

letters.org: National Association of Regulatory Utility Commissioners
letters.desc: At least 20 states have approved or pending large load tariffs with financial commitments, curtailment protocols, and minimum contract terms. NARUC supports preserving these state flexibility mechanisms rather than displacing them with federal rulemaking.
quotes: at least 20 states have approved or have pending large load tariffs or similar measures, which may include financial commitments, curtailment protocols, and minimum contract terms to allow for the rapid interconnection of large loads without compromising grid reliability or unduly burdening existing retail customers

letters.org: National Association of Regulatory Utility Commissioners
letters.desc: If FERC proposes reforms, NARUC wants them to permit flexibility, address the real challenges of large load interconnection, and account for regional and market structure diversity.
quotes: If the Commission proposes reforms, the reforms should permit flexibility and should address the real challenges currently facing the interconnection of large load
Any rule should provide for flexibility and should account for regional diversity and market structure diversity.

letters.desc: National Grid supports policies that incentivize large loads to accept curtailment or other flexibility commitments. Flexible loads can reduce or defer costly network upgrades, use existing capacity more efficiently, and accelerate interconnection timelines. Operational safeguards must accompany any flexibility arrangements.
quotes: Large loads that agree to be curtailable or otherwise flexible offer the potential to reduce costly network upgrades, make better use of existing transmission capacity, and accelerate interconnection timelines.

letters.desc: NRECA argues that regional differences in system configuration, load characteristics, and cooperative structure justify letting transmission providers set their own thresholds and study criteria rather than applying one national standard.
quotes: NRECA agrees that a lower-bound size limit on 'large loads' is necessary, but it opposes uniform, nationwide interconnection rules for all loads greater than 20 MW, which many electric cooperatives believe is too low.

the Commission should allow regional flexibility to establish a higher MW threshold, as well as different limits for different load characteristics and different transmission system configurations and conditions.

letters.org: Natural Resource Defense CouncilSustainable FERC ProjectClean Air Task Force ,Coalition for Affordable Utility Services and Energy Efficie ,EARTHJUSTICE ,ENVIRONMENTAL DEFENSE FUND ,MONTANA ENVIRONMENTAL INFORMATION CENTER ,Sierra Club ,Southern Environmental Law Center ,
letters.desc: The filers support flexibility and curtailment requirements as a condition for expedited interconnection, noting that even a 0.25% annual curtailment rate could integrate 76 GW of new load. Curtailment guidelines must, however, fairly allocate reliability risk at the wholesale level and must not force large loads to run backup generators in violation of air quality or run-time rules.
quotes: 76 GW of new load—equivalent to 10% of the nation's current aggregate peak demand—could be integrated with an average annual load curtailment rate of 0.25%.
FERC must establish guidelines to limit unfair allocation of reliability risks at the wholesale level.
any curtailment requirements must not allow a backup generator to be in violation of state or federal air quality laws or maximum backup generation run-time requirements.

letters.org: New York Independent System Operator, Inc.
letters.desc: NYISO strongly supports any final rule that allows ISOs and RTOs to adapt requirements to their own regional circumstances. It asks that the pro forma rule preserve independent entity variations and that timing requirements not be rigidly fixed, arguing that a one-size-fits-all approach risks disrupting existing processes, especially NYISO's recently implemented cluster study framework.
quotes: the NYISO urges the Commission to provide flexibility in how an ISO/RTO can address the rulemaking's requirements to account for the unique circumstances and challenges that exist in its regions.

If the Commission issues a notice of proposed rulemaking that includes pro forma language, the NYISO respectfully requests that the Commission continue to permit ISO/RTOs with the opportunity to seek "independent entity variations" to enable them to customize the proposed revisions as necessary to fit regional needs.

Affording flexibility to the NYISO to reform its load process will ensure that the timeliness of the generator interconnection process is not impacted while also furthering the goal of reliably interconnecting large loads to the transmission system fairly and expeditiously.

The NYISO encourages the Commission to afford each region the flexibility to propose appropriate timeframes and deadlines which reflect that particular region's required studies to identify reliability issues.
A pro forma rule that does not permit flexibility on the timing of the study process could cause delays to other NYISO study processes.

letters.org: New York Transmission OwnersCentral Hudson Gas & Electric CorporationNew York Power Authority ,New York State Electric & Gas Corp. and Rochester Gas and El ,Niagara Mohawk d/b/a/ National Grid ,Consolidated Edison Company of New York, Inc. and Orange and ,Long Island Power Authority ,
letters.desc: The NYTOs consistently ask that any federal requirements allow regions to tailor study paths, thresholds, and cost-allocation frameworks to local system characteristics. They oppose one-size-fits-all federal mandates and argue that preserving regional reform trajectories will accelerate, not slow, safe interconnections.
quotes: the NYTOs respectfully request that the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission ("FERC" or "the Commission") prioritize reliability, respect established jurisdictional boundaries, and permit regional flexibility to satisfy regional needs.

The 20 MW screen in Principle 2 should be treated as a planning indicator, not a jurisdictional trigger, so that regions can tailor applicability based on voltage, topology, and reliability considerations.

States, regions, and each Transmission Owner must retain discretion to set triggers that reflect local system characteristics and each Transmission Owner must have discretion to determine whether each customer is interconnecting at the transmission or distribution level under FERC's seven factor test.
Large-load requests should not be forced into generator cluster studies unless regional circumstances support doing so.

Load flexibility through curtailment alone is not sufficient to eliminate reliability impacts and justify interconnection prioritization when accounting for the magnitude of curtailment and that curtailment may not be obligatory or under NYISO dispatch as a demand side resource.

letters.desc: NERC supports integrating large data center loads while maintaining reliability, informed by prior grid events where loads amplified instability. The organization commits to interim guidance and parallel standards development to ensure loads contribute reliably to system operations.
quotes: we must stay laser-focused on reliability, informed by NERC's analysis of grid events in Virginia and Texas, where large data center loads have responded to, and amplified, grid instability.
We understand we must quickly secure the reliable contribution of these loads to the future system, especially given the lessons learned related to the integration of inverter-based resources.
The Level 2 Alert report also underscored the need for a Level 3 Alert to urge essential actions and provide guidance while registry criteria and Reliability Standards are modified.

A Level 3 Alert and guidance materials throughout 2026 via NERC and its subgroups will ensure that risk mitigation starts right away, while the appropriate regulatory process works to deliver the necessary updates to registration and standards.
NERC is committed to identifying and mitigating risks to the BPS so that the grid continues to support the North American economy and innovation.

NERC, in partnership with the Regional Entities, is committed to doing our part as the Electric Reliability Organization to enable the rapid growth of these key loads in a manner that preserves—and potentially enhances—reliability for all.

letters.desc: NCUC supports enhanced federal-state communication to ensure reliability while maintaining existing jurisdictional boundaries. The Commission agrees NERC's review of new registration categories and reliability standards is an appropriate avenue for addressing reliability concerns.
quotes: the NCUC supports enhanced federal-state communication to ensure reliability of the Bulk Electric System while respecting existing jurisdictional boundaries

letters.desc: Instead of curtailment-based expediting, NREMC supports fast-track interconnection for facilities paired with new front-of-meter generation where operational flexibility and system benefits are demonstrable. This maintains fairness and avoids distorting the interconnection queue.
quotes: A "fast-track" interconnection process should instead focus on facilities paired with new, front-of-meter generation, where operational flexibility and system benefits can be clearly demonstrated. This approach maintains fairness, supports reliable integration, and avoids preferential treatment that could distort the interconnection queue.

letters.org: Office of the Ohio Consumers' Counsel
letters.desc: OCC supports flexible interconnection rights for curtailable loads only when backed by telemetry verification and real penalties. Without enforcement, curtailable projects could behave as firm load while receiving preferential queue treatment.
quotes: any expedited connection process must be designed to protect consumers from inequitable queue treatment, hidden reliability costs, or cost shifting.
any expedited processing be contingent on enforceable curtailment and dispatchability commitment verified through telemetry and subject to penalties for non-performance.

letters.desc: ODEC states that the transition plan must ensure sufficient generation is available before large loads interconnect. Loads that connect before adequate capacity exists must accept curtailment obligations to protect system reliability and existing consumers.
quotes: Any transition plan must address resource adequacy for both system stability and consumer costs.

ODEC supports the encouragement of voluntary mechanisms to expedite interconnection studies, particularly for large loads that agree to be curtailable and for hybrid facilities that agree to be curtailable and dispatchable. However, these expedited processes must not compromise system reliability or allow standards to fall below acceptable levels.

letters.desc: OpenAI supports an optional curtailable-load pathway and argues loads that agree to curtail on operator call should get interconnection priority over inflexible loads.
quotes: OpenAIsupportsanoptionalcurtailable-loadpathwaywherefullorpartialcurtailment obligations of the large loads allow thetransmissionprovidertoexpeditetheinterconnection request.
Largeloadsthatagreetocurtaildemandwhencalledonbysystemoperatorsfor a predetermined number of hours should be given interconnection priority over inflexible loads.

letters.desc: OpenAI supports enabling AI data centers with load flexibility and demand response to serve as grid assets during emergencies. The filer argues that flexible facilities reduce peak infrastructure needs, improve reliability, and unlock capacity constrained by outdated planning.
quotes: Grid Flexibility can unlock substantial capacity currently constrained by outdated peak-demand planning.

AI data centers, in particular, could function as assets capable of supporting the grid when it is under emergency conditions, such as during times of extreme heat or cold (which typically would put stress on the grid)—when they are paired with generation, load-flexibility, and demand response.
If these AI data centers can reduce consumption during peak periods, such facilities could trim the need for incremental infrastructure, and improve overall reliability.

A framework that enables Grid Flexibility, integrates co-located generation and storage, aligns cost responsibility with national infrastructure benefits, and enforces consistent timelines will not only protect the grid—it will help unlock the next era of American reindustrialization, technological leadership, and democratic economic growth.
Every AI facility can serve not only as a compute hub, but also as a testbed for energy innovation that strengthens the grid and accelerates clean, reliable baseload development.

letters.desc: Oracle asks FERC to harmonize load shedding practices and downtime calculations across regions, arguing that the current patchwork of standards creates unnecessary friction for data center operators.
quotes: The Commission should support efforts to streamline administrative procedures and harmonize standards related to load sheds and down time.
the Commission could encourage ways to harmonize load shedding practices as well as downtime calculations.

letters.desc: Oracle supports streamlined regulatory processes and modernization to enable large-load customers to integrate self-generated power into the grid. The company argues that regulatory modernization would facilitate direct partnerships with utilities and transmission operators on commercial terms.
quotes: Oracle strongly supports the White House's commitment to win the 'race to achieve global dominance in artificial intelligence (AI)' and encourages the Commission to bolster U.S. AI dominance by streamlining processes and incentivizing growth for infrastructure deployment both in the United States and in trusted partner/allied nations.

Modernizing the regulatory framework could allow large-load customers that self-generate electricity to more directly partner with utilities, transmission infrastructure owners, and others to make excess capacity available to the grid on commercial reasonable terms.

letters.desc: OMS views load flexibility as critical to accelerating interconnection while keeping the grid affordable and reliable for existing customers. It conditions support on adequate cost allocation safeguards.
quotes: FERC should confirm that interconnection under this framework does not confer a right to self-procure from wholesale markets, except through approved arrangements such as co-location or behind-the-meter generation used for flexibility or demand-response purposes.
enabling load flexibility is critical to accelerating the interconnection of large loads while maintaining a reliable and affordable grid for existing customers.

as the Commission develops proposed requirements for flexible or co-located loads, it should ensure potential changes to existing regulatory constructs, public engagement processes, cost allocation frameworks, wholesale markets, and transmission planning are sufficiently stringent to shield existing customers from negative impacts and to determine whether the large loads are paying for the grid services they use (transmission, ancillary services, reliability backstop, etc.).

letters.desc: Paces supports tying the fastest interconnection track to loads that are dispatchable or curtailable, treating flexibility as a prerequisite for expedited treatment rather than an optional feature.
quotes: sited at buses with positive headroom and nearby developable land

letters.desc: PG&E consistently asks for flexibility rather than one-size-fits-all mandates: on study coordination, expedited queue rules, cost responsibility frameworks, and implementation timelines.
quotes: PG&E believes that three key principles are essential to any final Commission rule: Protecting existing ratepayers from incurring additional or stranded costs while also adopting fair and equitable cost responsibility and allocation approaches for large load customers; Appropriately balancing state and Commission jurisdiction and developing a complimentary and cooperative framework, while also ensuring timely state action on large load issues; and Developing clear rules that will expedite large load interconnections by allowing flexibility rather than imposing additional requirements that slow the interconnection process.

the Commission should not adopt a blanket rule that large loads and hybrid facilities offering curtailment/dispatchability always receive expedited consideration. There may be situations where a utility or transmission provider has limited transmission planning resources and those resources are already fully committed to studying interconnections which were previously submitted and have been pending for some time.

The Commission should avoid a one-size-fits-all approach to cost responsibility and refunds especially given the unique rate structures and designs in each state. Instead, the Commission should allow utilities and/or states to develop a cost responsibility and refund proposal that is right for that utility and/or state.

letters.org: Pennsylvania Office of Consumer AdvocateDelaware Division of the Public AdvocateIllinois Office of Attorney General ,
letters.desc: The filers support flexible or curtailable interconnection options but insist curtailment must be tied to causal responsibility: loads that caused resource inadequacy should bear curtailment risk first. Any flexibility commitment must be enforceable without event-count caps.
quotes: curtailments should protect current customers, especially residential consumers, over new large load customers that cause the resource inadequacy

FERC can and should recognize that RTOs must depart from pro-rata transmission curtailment in the rare circumstances where (1) the large loads have caused the resource inadequacy; and (2) the RTO has (a) exhausted all of its options for avoiding transmission curtailment of customers, and (b) has established that those transmission customers that would be disproportionately affected by the curtailment – new large loads – have options to reduce their need for transmission capacity, including alternative supply options, compensation for demand response, or reduced transmission rates for the interruptible service they are provided.

any curtailable or dispatchable commitments made by large loads and hybrid facilities must be verifiable, enforceable, and subject to penalties for non-performance. There should not be limits on the number of curtailable events or the number of times for curtailments as some request.

letters.desc: Data centers cause sudden, unpredictable megawatt-scale load surges. RTOs must have authority to impose forced curtailment requirements on large loads to maintain grid reliability.
quotes: Public Citizen raised concerns about the disruptive impact large loads were having on grid reliability, particularly the manner in which data centers feature sudden and unpredictable surges of hundreds or thousands of megawatts coming on- or offline at once.
Subjecting data centers to federal reliability standards should include a requirement for RTOs to impose forced curtailment requirements on large loads as a tool to ensure grid reliability.

letters.desc: RSI's proposed rule would cover load that plans to provide demand flexibility and sell it into wholesale markets, recognizing that such arrangements reduce the need for additional capacity and network transmission.
quotes: FERC should conduct a rulemaking permitting Commission-jurisdictional interconnection processes for load, but only where the interconnection is necessary to offer or receive an otherwise wholesale market service.

accelerating the interconnection of these load-and-FERC-jurisdictional-service configurations is warranted, given their outsized contribution to resource adequacy and limiting the impact on the broader transmission network.

letters.desc: Large loads should use aggregated distributed energy resources and demand flexibility to meet interconnection requirements. Off-site DERs can deliver equivalent grid benefits as co-located generation and should be evaluated on performance location within the same constrained area, not physical site.
quotes: There is also significant latent capacity and flexibility in existing, readily deployable distributed resources that can be mobilized far faster than new generation or major network upgrades.
Off-site distributed energy resources can deliver the same types of energy services—generation, load reduction, or transmission relief—that on-site assets provide.

Large loads should therefore be allowed to incorporate aggregated front-of-the-meter and behind-the-meter DERs into their interconnection applications to the extent those resources can offset the transmission or generation upgrades triggered by the request.
A long-term commitment to secure and maintain such contributions should be treated comparably to co-located generation for modeling purposes.

FERC should expand its expedited interconnection considerations beyond large load curtailability and co-located generation dispatchability to include appropriately located off-site distributed energy resources that can deliver curtailment or dispatch services under contract.

what matters is equivalent, verifiable performance in mitigating constraints within the same constrained transmission pocket or local grid area, not whether the asset is physically inside or outside the facility fence line.

By allowing both durable peak reductions and aggregated distributed flexibility to qualify under Principles 3 and 7, FERC can give large loads more options to meet interconnection requirements quickly, affordably, and reliably.

letters.desc: Rewiring America emphasizes that DERs and virtual power plants provide cost-effective, dispatchable, location-targeted grid services deployable at scale and warrant consideration under the reform principles. Performance-based frameworks should ensure flexibility resources are eligible and credited for transmission relief.
quotes: DERs and virtual power plants increasingly provide cost-effective, dispatchable, and location-targeted grid services that can be deployed quickly at scale, making their treatment under Principles 34 and 75 an important consideration for the Commission.

A performance-based approach to concurrent study and expedited large load interconnection ensures that flexibility resources are eligible and credited for providing transmission relief, while remaining technology-neutral and consistent with Order 2222.

letters.desc: Shell Energy asks that rules avoid mandates or barriers that could suppress price signals, and that ongoing regional program development continue alongside the federal rulemaking. New rules should use existing market tools where possible to speed implementation.
quotes: The principles should not be requirements for large loads to interconnect under permanent operational restrictions; instead, should be interpreted as options that can expedite initial interconnections and allow for interim operations while full studies and transmission construction activities are completed if large loads need full grid access.

Shell Energy believes hybrid/co-located load and generation facilities should retain the right to request future study and full market participation without system protection facilities or system protection schemes limiting injection and withdrawal to low net MW values, where full grid access better suits their long-run operational needs, or after necessary network upgrades enter service.
The rulemaking process should not impede the ongoing development of regional programs, tariffs, and procedures that support the objectives outlined in the ANOPR.
Ensure the new rules do not disrupt market price signals and misalign with established market principles.

letters.desc: Sierra Club urges FERC to encourage policies that bring clean, low-cost energy technologies such as solar, wind, battery storage, and geothermal online to serve rising demand from large loads, treating clean energy as both the affordability and reliability answer.
quotes: FERC should encourage policies to ensure that the lowest-cost energy technologies, including abundant, clean energy like solar, wind, battery power, and geothermal come online to match rising electric demand and ensure grid reliability.

letters.desc: SMA supports flexibility and curtailability requirements, arguing its inverter technology already meets these demands. Controllability should be measured at the interconnection point, not at individual components, to give owners maximum implementation flexibility.
quotes: Controllability (in particular curtailability and dispatchability) with SMA technology is already field-proven and state-of-the-art (system operators can manage it) using, for example, the IEEE 2030.5 (SEP2) protocol.
Preferably, controllability should be assessed at the interconnection point rather than at individual components, allowing owners maximum flexibility in implementation.

SMA suggests allowing a 'priority setup' to be connected, where facilities with their own infrastructure that already supports grid stability - such as BESS with advanced grid-forming capabilities - can provide all relevant ancillary services and receive appropriate incentives (e.g. compensation fees or easy connection process).

letters.desc: SEIA urges the Commission to make the pro forma Large Load Interconnection Service Agreement adaptable to different load configurations, including fully islanded loads, loads with firm backup service, and flexible loads that can respond to price signals or participate in demand response. Study assumptions should reflect each load's actual operational profile.
quotes: any study of the large load and associated generation, whether co-located or not, must reflect the actual operational needs of the load.
SEIA does not support this principle. The Commission should not require load that agrees to be curtailable to be explicitly expedited.

letters.desc: MISO's Expedited Project Review process quickly approves transmission projects needed for urgent reliability, including many large load additions, demonstrating that speed and jurisdiction need not conflict.
quotes: Like SPP, MISO has worked to facilitate the interconnection of large loads on its system. MISO established a mechanism, known as the Expedited Project Review process, to quickly study and approve transmission projects that are necessary to meet urgent reliability requirements, many of which are associated with large load additions.

letters.org: Southern Company Services, Inc.Alabama Power CompanyGeorgia Power Company ,Mississippi Power Company ,
letters.desc: The filing argues that a prescriptive national rule would burden regions already achieving timely interconnections, requiring them to seek compliance variances and inviting litigation. A narrower approach built on guidance, best practices, or minimum principles is presented as more durable and less disruptive to successful regional models.
quotes: many parties have expressed concern that progress already made could be undermined if the Commission were to enact an overly prescriptive final rule.
FERC should consider adopting broad principles that allow for innovation and regional flexibility, rather than narrow prescriptions.

establishing a national standard would require those regions that are already successfully interconnecting large loads to seek a variance through the Commission's compliance process, which could be time-consuming, burdensome, and litigious, ultimately slowing interconnections rather than accelerating the goals of the ANOPR.
A narrower approach—focused on guidance, best practices, or minimum principles—offers a more durable, timely, and legally sustainable path.

Southern Companies argued that the Commission could achieve the objectives of the ANOPR by using lessons learned from this proceeding to establish a list of national best practices for large load interconnections and adopt a policy statement or similar vehicle to encourage the use of these best practices.

letters.org: Southern Company Services, Inc.Alabama Power CompanyGeorgia Power Company ,Mississippi Power Company ,
letters.desc: Southern Companies argue regional differences justify preserving flexibility for frameworks already delivering timely infrastructure, and that a one-size-fits-all rule would be counterproductive. They suggest any near-term reforms focus on regions where wholesale markets and Commission-jurisdictional processes are directly implicated.
quotes: Southern Companies’ experience demonstrates that coordinated state-regulated planning structures can support more timely generation development and reduce interconnection delays relative to regions currently experiencing substantial queue backlogs and infrastructure constraints.  These differing regional conditions support preserving flexibility for frameworks already providing coordinated and timely infrastructure development.
We respectfully suggest that any federal initiative that comes from this proceeding preserve well-functioning state-led frameworks that can help deliver speed and affordability.

Given the success of state-regulated integrated resource planning and bundled retail service frameworks in integrating large load customers, such as in Southern Companies’ territories, a one-size-fits-all rule would be counterproductive.

Any federal reforms adopted in this proceeding should preserve the flexibility for states and vertically integrated utilities to continue to use coordinated bundled-service structures that are already delivering timely infrastructure development, customer protections, and reliable service.

To the extent the Commission determines that additional near-term federal reforms are appropriate, those reforms should focus principally on regions where wholesale market structures, transmission service constructs, and Commission-jurisdictional processes are directly implicated.

letters.desc: SMECO emphasizes that control mechanisms for dispatchable large loads must be adequate for PJM to integrate such facilities into both operations and system planning.
quotes: SMECO respectfully submits that a final rule to establish standardized, non-discriminatory procedures for "orderly" interconnections of large new loads without compromising reliability is needed at the present time.

SMECO urges the Commission, in any final rule, to ensure that PJM's ability to control such eligible load facilities through curtailment and/or dispatch, through, for example PJM Price Responsive Demand and Demand response products, to the extent those or similar products is permitted at all to serve new large loads, is adequate for PJM to integrate the facility into both operations and system planning.

letters.desc: SPP's central ask is that FERC allow each RTO/ISO and its stakeholders to design their own large load interconnection rules rather than impose a single national standard. This applies to thresholds, study timelines, study methods, and curtailment priority.
quotes: SPP encourages the Commission to provide flexibility in any rules adopted based on the vast regional differences across the country. Rather than pursuing a "one-size fits all" approach, the Commission should consider allowing each Regional Transmission Organization ("RTO") and Independent System Operator ("ISO") ("RTO/ISO") and its stakeholders the latitude to design for these differences.

SPP requests that any final rules in this matter do not include any specific MW threshold, but instead, the final rules should allow each transmission provider to propose thresholds specific to the needs of their transmission systems.

Any load connected to the SPP Transmission System, including load that agrees to be curtailed, will require energy to be produced and will take some capacity from the Transmission System; otherwise, they would not need to connect to the grid. Even when agreeing to curtail, a curtailable, or non-firm load, will impact existing and future firm load and should not be prioritized over a load that is willing to bring, or already has Designated Resources.
SPP suggests allowing each region to determine the best approach to minimize the time of study.

letters.desc: Splight advocates capacity allocation proportional to load response speed and magnitude. The company argues that fast-responding loads offer an alternative to traditional network expansion, enabling the system to operate near full capacity while maintaining N-1 planning criteria and potentially doubling interconnection capacity through contingent allocation.
quotes: Splight strongly supports this principle and respectfully urges the Commission to go further by explicitly recognizing the value of large loads that implement advanced, automated contingency response technologies ("Fast-Responding Loads") as a basis for both (1) expedited interconnection and (2) allocation of increased capacity in proportional to the speed and amount of curtailment a load is able to provide.

By incorporating this advanced responsiveness, Fast-Responding Loads allow the system to operate at up to the full physical capacity of the grid, except in the rare event of a system failure, thus freeing enough of the system capacity to serve double the amount of demand interconnected.

Allowing qualified large loads to directly manage and implement RAS actions such as dynamic load reduction (in cooperation with their utility), would improve reliability and accelerate infrastructure development without compromising bulk electric system security.

letters.desc: SMA argues that EAF steel mills can shed 80 percent of load within minutes, providing grid benefits that distinguish them from other large loads and support differentiated treatment under interconnection rules.
quotes: An opt out would also recognize the contrasting demand-response capacity, and attendant benefits, of loads such as electric arc furnace steel manufacturers, which can shed 80% of load with several minutes notice.

letters.desc: Terraflux wants interconnection customers to define their own net amounts and to submit two alternative net-amount scenarios studied concurrently, enabling right-sizing of hybrid facility components.
quotes: FERC should allow the interconnection customer to indicate what those net amounts will be, rather than the grid operator assuming full nameplate of load and full nameplate of generation is netted from one another. Secondly, FERC should allow the customer to provide two additional, alternative 'net amounts scenarios' to also be studied, concurrent with the first scenario, which would allow the customer to right-size its hybrid facility components between facility needs and grid capacity.

letters.desc: Tesla supports mechanisms that limit duplicative load interconnection requests, and argues readiness and study-deposit requirements should target large loads presumed to be data centers or crypto mining centers.
quotes: Tesla is generally supportive of concepts that limit duplicative load interconnection requests; however, we believe that requirements should be instituted for large loads presumed to be data centers or crypto mining centers.

Tesla believes that capacity additions behind the same POI that offset generation “loss” to serve load should be permitted with expedited reviews, assuming the system maintains consistent or similar POI import/export limitations.

letters.desc: The filing's central argument is that bitcoin mining and AI compute loads can curtail in seconds and should qualify for a dedicated non-firm interconnection pathway. The filer argues this differs fundamentally from always-on load, reduces upgrade requirements, and benefits grid reliability. SPP's HILLS program is cited as a proven template.
quotes: not all large loads behave the same way. Digital-compute data centers, particularly bitcoin mining and, in the future, some emerging AI compute installations, can operate as large, flexible, interruptible loads with the capability to modulate power consumption within seconds in response to grid demands.
we recommend that DOE support the creation and adoption of a non-firm load interconnection category across U.S. markets.
Southwest Power Pool's (SPP) High-Impact Large Loads (HILLs) framework enables "fast-track" interconnection for large loads that agree to curtail when needed to preserve reliability.

Flexible load does not require the same level of transmission upgrades as other businesses and often locates at or near existing power sources. This reduces required studies, transmission upgrades, and queue congestion.

Bitcoin mining facilities in Texas have already demonstrated real-time load shed performance ahead of grid emergencies, contributing meaningful stability during both extreme heat and winter reliability events.

When these loads are exposed to real-time prices and congestion signals, they shift consumption away from peak periods using a variety of market-based tools, reducing uplift charges and lessening the need for emergency procurement.
Encourage FERC-jurisdictional ISOs and RTOs as well as ERCOT to establish a uniform, non-firm interconnection category for qualifying flexible loads.

letters.desc: VPPs provide modular, scalable flexibility that responds dynamically to system conditions and delivers verifiable reductions in net peak demand. This supports the show-cause-order's flexibility principles.
quotes: VPPs are inherently modular and flexible, allowing them to scale rapidly, respond dynamically to system conditions, and provide verifiable reductions to a load's net peak demand.

By establishing a framework and appropriate ground rules for allowing VPPs to be studied together with load and hybrid facilities, the Commission can ensure that large loads have a diverse suite of tools for flexibility and resource adequacy, accelerate interconnection timelines, and encourage large loads to make DER investments that can simultaneously provide direct consumer savings and resiliency benefits.

letters.desc: Pew argues VPPs should be explicitly included in any flexibility framework the Commission adopts. They can curtail or dispatch to reduce transmission system impacts, are faster to deploy than utility-scale resources, and enable a broader range of large load customers to qualify for expedited interconnection pathways.
quotes: large load customers and hybrid facilities to be able to contract with VPPs and to have those contracts accounted for within the scope of interconnection procedures would greatly further DOE's goals, while advancing the Commission's statutory mandate and principles of facilitating resource-neutral competition in wholesale markets.
the Commission cannot afford not to deploy this important tool. Rather, it should insist that transmission providers include it within the toolbox and use it for the job at hand.

Adopting rules that allow integrated, expedited study of large loads that contract with VPPs will facilitate speed-to-power for large load customers while keeping transmission and energy affordable for existing customers.

VPPs, by contrast, do not depend on proceeding through the large generator interconnection queue. As Distributed Capacity Parties explain, '[d]istributed capacity assets are installed today across critical footprints, are readily installable en masse, and may be aggregated into utility-scale assets on a timeline of months rather than years'

[W]hat matters is equivalent, verifiable performance in mitigating constraints within the same constrained transmission pocket or local grid area, not whether the asset is physically inside or outside the facility fence line.

the Commission should define hybrid facility in a manner that includes large loads paired with VPPs and/or allow for large load customers and hybrid facilities to contract with VPPs or coordinate operations with jointly-owned VPPs in order to provide curtailment and/or dispatch capability.

the Commission should adopt resource-neutral definitions that allow VPPs to satisfy technical requirements where they are able to provide the services that the technical requirements are designed to ensure.
Aggregated DERs, again, should be eligible as 'adjacent supply' in this example, because they are as able to reduce the new large load's transmission system impacts as utility-scale resources.
VPPs are critically positioned to allow the timely interconnection of large loads while protecting existing customers from adverse impacts and allowing for additional benefits.

Pew urges the Commission to draft its rules in such a way that unlocks the multiple benefits that VPPs can provide both to existing transmission customers and large load customers seeking to interconnect while keeping electricity rates affordable and maintaining grid reliability.

letters.desc: TBA calls for queue priority and streamlined study timelines for loads that commit to peak avoidance and operator-directed curtailment. Asset-backed flexibility lowers system risk during stress periods, justifying accelerated review. Non-firm service should be available so flexible loads can interconnect without securing network resources.
quotes: Allowing large flexible loads the ability to connect expeditiously, manage their wholesale risks and commit to dispatchability will support a more affordable, resilient grid for all customers.
The Commission should require transmission providers to provide such loads with expedited interconnection treatment by giving them queue priority.

Queue priority is appropriate because loads that can demonstrate asset-backed flexibility pose substantially lower system risks during periods of grid stress and should therefore be eligible for accelerated review.

Flexible loads that select non-firm service and can avoid peak loads should receive reduced interconnection and transmission upgrade requirements, and should avoid all network resource and resource adequacy/capacity requirements.

letters.desc: TBA's central ask is a mandatory non-firm network transmission service option at every jurisdictional transmission provider. The filing argues that flexible loads like thermal energy storage can curtail during peaks and therefore should not be treated as firm, and that a Commission directive is needed to prevent a regional patchwork. SPP's CHILLS and PALS are cited as proof of administrative feasibility.
quotes: commenters overwhelmingly agree that large loads capable of providing durable, enforceable flexibility should be eligible for expedited interconnection pathways
such expedited treatment is only feasible when the interconnecting load takes service on a non‑firm or conditional basis
TBA urges the Commission to require every jurisdictional transmission provider to offer at least one non‑firm network transmission service option tailored to large flexible loads

only loads that are "completely curtailable or dispatchable" should qualify for expedited interconnection study treatment, underscoring that the depth of flexibility determines whether a project can be evaluated without peak-driven upgrades

SPP's comments provide perhaps the clearest illustration of workable non-firm constructs, as the RTO is already pursuing tariff revisions to create the Conditional High Impact Large Load Service ("CHILLS") and the Price Adaptive Load Service ("PALS")
a Commission requirement is needed to ensure that all transmission providers offer such a product, rather than relying on voluntary regional experimentation
carefully tailored guidelines that set forth clear minimum standards for non-firm transmission service offerings would offer significant benefits
non-firm eligibility must be tied to tangible operational characteristics
SPP or the Transmission Owner may curtail load "during critical peaking grid events," and the customer must comply immediately or face unreserved-use penalties

letters.desc: Tract backs expedited study for loads offering curtailability or dispatchability as a tool to reduce system impact and speed interconnection.
quotes: Tract agrees with the proposal to expedite the interconnection study of large loads that agree to be curtailable and hybrid facilities that agree to be curtailable and dispatchable.

letters.desc: The Coalition supports expediting interconnection for curtailable and dispatchable large loads and hybrid facilities. It argues storage is the fastest way to make loads flexible and that storage-backed loads can interconnect with minimal system impact, justifying faster study timelines.
quotes: The ANOPR’s proposal to expedite interconnection studies for large loads and hybrid facilities that agree to be curtailable and dispatchable can, if implemented effectively, significantly increase the pace of interconnection for large loads and their associated supply resources.
Energy storage is uniquely positioned as a rapid pathway for making loads curtailable and flexible, enabling them to potentially seek and obtain expedited interconnection.

Enabling large loads to avoid drawing from the grid by maintaining dispatchable energy during peak demand events—when transmission constraints are most salient—can dramatically reduce or eliminate the need for network upgrades that would otherwise require years of study and construction (as well as sizeable costs) to accommodate.

the Commission should ensure in any final action that storage resources are permitted to charge in low-usage intervals, when doing so will not trigger the need for expensive and long-lead-time upgrades that could easily place loads behind their planned interconnection schedules.

These limited withdrawal rights should be applicable in defined, constrained intervals, that will enable flexibility while also providing clarity regarding which constraints are binding, and which actions are needed to avoid any adverse impacts.

On the load side, major considerations include the percentage of load that must be curtailable, how many hours annually a load must be flexible, what response times are required, and whether curtailability commitments must be firm or may be conditional on operational constraints.
Without objective criteria, transmission providers will apply inconsistent standards, and developers will face regulatory uncertainty that undermines the benefits of expedited processing.

letters.desc: UCS supports expedited interconnection for curtailable and dispatchable large loads but says the principle is unworkable without explicit rules specifying duration and quantity of curtailment commitments. The filing recommends designating both supply and load from hybrid customers as non-firm and subject to economic dispatch, consistent with existing Order 888 practices for non-firm transmission service.
quotes: the Commission should propose rules that both supply (in the case of a hybrid interconnection) and the load will need to commit to respond to operator dispatch instructions. That commitment should indicate both the duration and the quantity of the response, in either megawatts or percentage of the injection and withdrawal rights.

Any forthcoming rule from the Commission must include criteria for determining the amount and the duration of curtailment and/or dispatch to avoid controversy and delay in the adoption of this principle.

The most direct approach compatible with existing grid operator dispatch is to have both the supply and demand from such interconnection customers be designated as non-firm and subject to economic dispatch.

letters.desc: The Congress members point to near-miss outage events caused by data center clusters suddenly disconnecting, and ask FERC to authorize utility-administered curtailment protocols for grid emergencies. They frame controlled curtailment as a reliability safeguard, not just a cost tool.
quotes: there have been "near miss" incidents in regions with rigorous data center buildout which have raised concerns about black outs when clusters of data centers have suddenly dropped off the grid.
Authorizing utility-administered curtailment protocols during grid emergencies.

letters.desc: Verrus contends that current rules treat all large loads as cost drivers and ignore the reliability value of engineered, asset-backed flexibility. FERC should require RTOs and transmission providers to model and compensate flexible load curtailment as a reliability resource in planning and cost allocation.
quotes: Flexible large loads represent a technology solution that can uniquely speed interconnection time, maximize the use of the grid we have, while also providing a distinct set of benefits to grid operators and resource adequacy planners.

Today, the benefits of load flexibility are neither accounted for nor compensated. As a result, flexible resources are discouraged from the market and cannot practically be used to accelerate interconnection times or to protect consumers from the costs of load growth.

The Commission should establish a clear, standardized definition of 'flexible load' as an asset-backed, verifiable, and dispatchable demand capable of modulating consumption in coordination with the transmission provider or balancing authority throughout a long-term commitment.

Flexibility must be physical, durable, and measurable—not merely theoretical or price-responsive. The defining characteristic should be the presence of on-site assets such as battery energy storage, power-flow controls, or other infrastructure that enables sustained, repeatable flexibility over decades, not just seasonal participation.

The Commission should require a Fast-Lane Study Track for verified flexible loads, using shorter study timelines and modeling that accounts for their ability to curtail or shift load and to operate on-site resources.
