Verrus respects the long-standing role of the PJM Independent Market Monitor in safeguarding competitive markets, but disagrees with recent assertions that flexible data centers are a 'regulatory fiction.' That characterization reflects an older conception of demand response as voluntary or behavioral.

Traditional demand response typically depends on customer willingness, has limited duration, and can vary year to year. In contrast, asset-backed flexible data centers incorporate physical infrastructure—utility-scale battery storage, automated curtailment systems, real-time telemetry, and programmable power distribution—that enables predictable, dispatchable performance over the full life of the interconnection agreement.

letters.desc: Verrus urges FERC to create a formal Flexible Load subclass for asset-backed loads that commit to material, verifiable curtailment. The filing argues the current one-size-fits-all framework unjustly treats grid-supportive and grid-stressing loads identically, and proposes a threshold of the greater of 20 MW or 25% of total load for qualification. Verrus rejects the 100% curtailability bar some commenters propose as unnecessarily restrictive.
quotes: the current "one-size-fits-all" approach to large load interconnection is unjust, unreasonable, and unduly discriminatory.
Existing rules generally fail to distinguish between loads that strain the grid and loads that possess the physical capability to support it.

the current framework forces flexible loads to cross-subsidize inflexible ones, requiring customers who can operationally avoid the need for network upgrades to pay for infrastructure that is only necessary for their inflexible peers.

it forces these agile resources to wait in queues behind projects requiring years of costly upgrades, rather than allowing them to connect quickly by leveraging the underutilized non-peak grid capacity already in place.
a load should qualify for the "Flexible" subclass (and the associated fast-lane study) if it commits to curtailing the greater of 20 MW or 25% of its total load.

Insisting on 100% curtailability would strand significant value. A facility that can curtail 50% or even 25% of a massive load could still offer hundreds of megawatts of relief to the system—relief that can avoid upgrades and improve reliability.

Verrus agrees with the California Independent System Operator ("CAISO") and Transmission Access Policy Study Group ("TAPS") that "strict, unwavering protections" are necessary to ensure that flexible loads meet their curtailment obligations.

Treating a flexible project that requires zero network upgrades with the same study duration as a massive, inflexible load that requires new transmission lines is, in itself, discriminatory. It delays the efficient project for no technical reason.

When a technical pathway exists to interconnect large loads quickly—because they do not require network upgrades—requiring them to proceed at the pace of the slowest, most complex projects is a policy error the country cannot afford.

It could create a separate "Flexible Large Load" interconnection class with distinct processes and transmission service cost structures, or establish separate classes of transmission service (e.g., conditional firm service) that large loads can select.

letters.desc: The VSCC notes that Virginia and many other states are actively working on data center load flexibility and demand-side programs. A cooperative approach would allow these state-level efforts to continue and expand, while a federal takeover would preempt them.
quotes: The Commission should enable the accelerated interconnection of large loads that are willing to bring their own generation or to be co-located with generation by creating a fast-track generator interconnection queue for those verified generation resources, such as PJM's existing Commission-approved Reliability Resource Initiative.

the interconnection study of large loads that agree to be curtailable and hybrid facilities that agree to be curtailable and dispatchable should be expedited. Many states, including Virginia, are currently addressing data center load flexibility, and a cooperative approach in this proceeding would allow these efforts to proceed.

letters.desc: The VSCC proposes that loads willing to commit to reliable, predictable curtailment during critical operating conditions should be eligible for the same voluntary fast-track pathway as co-located loads.
quotes: FERC should establish the criteria for eligible large load interconnections to voluntarily enter a separate queue when they can demonstrate system impact mitigation through co-location, curtailment, or a combination of both.

letters.desc: Vistra supports using curtailability as an incentive mechanism -- loads that agree to be curtailable would receive expedited interconnection access -- as a substitute for burdening the interconnection process with resource adequacy analysis.
quotes: the Commission could incentivize loads to agree to be curtailable through expedited interconnection access.

letters.desc: The filers urge FERC to direct RTOs/ISOs to expedite studies for large loads that bring curtailable or dispatchable distributed assets, and to broaden Principle Seven so it counts incremental distributed capacity such as load flexibility, storage, and generation. They want all available resources, not only traditional generation, recognized in the reform.
quotes: the Distributed Capacity Parties respectfully urge the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (“FERC” or “Commission”) in any subsequent rulemaking2 to direct the Regional Transmission Organizations/Independent System Operators (“RTO/ISOs”) to develop mechanisms for granting expedited interconnection studies to large loads that provide curtailable and/or dispatchable distributed assets

The ANOPR Seventh Principle4 should include incremental Distributed Capacity in the form of load flexibility, storage, and/or generation capacity whose location can address capacity and transmission constraints projected to be caused by the new large loads, even if such capacity is located on the distribution system.
ANOPR Principle Seven should be broadened to leverage all available resources.

letters.desc: Off-site DERs, VPPs, and adjacent aggregated resources deliver the same generation, load reduction, and transmission relief services as on-site assets. Flexible technologies including demand response and coordinated resource aggregations should be recognized as equivalent providers of system support.
quotes: can be distributed across the geographic area within which the new load will impact system constraints, provided that the system operator has the requisite level of control to integrate the facility into operations and system planning.
Off-site distributed energy resources ("DERs") can deliver the same types of energy services—generation, load reduction, or transmission relief—that on-site assets provide.
The defining feature of resource adequacy is dispatchability, not geography.

such adjacent flexibility refers to the ability to coordinate with nearby or aggregated resources (e.g., a local VPP) via a software interface, so that the net effect reduces withdrawals on constrained parts of the grid.
VPPs should be considered for their potential to alleviate transmission network constraints and capacity needs associated with the interconnection of large loads.

letters.desc: The UTC supports FERC developing principles for prioritizing load flexibility that states can apply within their own processes. However, any curtailable or dispatchable interconnection framework must align with Washington's Climate Commitment Act and Clean Energy Transformation Act.
quotes: we encourage the development of principles of how to prioritize load flexibility in interconnection processes. These principles can be applied in state processes across the country to further develop policies that will advance interconnection of large loads while protecting reliability and affordability.

the process and timing for dispatchable and curtailable interconnection would need to align with Washington's Climate Commitment Act and Clean Energy Transformation Act as highlighted by the findings and recommendations adopted by Washington state's Data Center Working Group

letters.desc: The filers note that when large load interconnection agreements include load flexibility provisions, DLR becomes especially valuable by reducing the hours requiring curtailment.
quotes: If the interconnection agreement includes load flexibility, DLR will be even more valuable in reducing the number of hours requiring load curtailment.

letters.desc: The filer contends that transmission owners currently lack staff and processes dedicated to grid efficiency, and urges the Commission to direct operational planning reforms. It recommends monthly, quarterly, and yearly efficiency analyses that incorporate GETs, arguing these can unlock latent capacity within two to three years.
quotes: accelerated ATT adoption is more likely to speed the interconnection of new large loads to constrained transmission systems rather than frustrate speed to power goals.
very few, if any, transmission owners have employees in engineering or operations roles where one of their primary job responsibilities is to ensure efficient grid operation.

We urge the Commission to act, through a policy statement or order directing reports, to encourage transmission owners and RTOs to develop processes focused on improving grid efficiency. These processes could unlock latent grid capacity in the timescales needed to win the AI race–the next two to three years—as well as to address the growing affordability crisis.

letters.desc: ACORE is wary that prioritizing curtailable or flexible loads through queue prioritization could disrupt processing of generation needed to meet growing demand.
quotes: ACORE is concerned that queue prioritization methods can disrupt the processing of needed generation waiting in lengthy interconnection queues.

letters.desc: The filer accepts the concept of expedited treatment for curtailable large load customers but opposes a blanket mandate for shorter study timelines. Any study priority must be tied to binding curtailment obligations at meaningful levels, not token commitments designed to game the system.
quotes: Rather than mandating a shorter study period for curtailable customers, the Commission could instead consider providing a study priority for curtailable large load customers relative to other large load customers, but limited to those large load customers that make a binding and enforceable commitment to offer a meaningful level of curtailment.

letters.desc: ITI supports expedited study for flexible loads but opposes mandatory prioritization based on curtailment ability as potentially discriminatory. Curtailment must be voluntary, and clear operational guidelines are needed because not all loads can shift flexibly and backup generators face air and noise permit constraints.
quotes: ITI agrees that hybrid projects and large loads that agree to be flexible according to operational standards that result in fewer transmission or generation investments would lead to reduced energization timelines. However, the prioritization of study queues based on the ability to be curtailable may lead to inconsistent policy priorities and raise significant questions around non-discriminatory and non-preferential access.

Regulators should take into account the complexity of this issue in practice, and curtailment should be voluntary and not mandatory. Not all large loads are able to reduce their load flexibly and shift load across time or geographic areas. Sometimes, curtailing load from the grid involves firing backup generators, which are bound by existing air permit laws and noise control. Clear guidelines are needed to define the amount of flexibility and the duration of response expected.

letters.desc: IECA opposes making curtailability a condition of expedited interconnection, arguing that excluding non-curtailable loads would harm the public interest. At the same time, it supports FERC encouraging large loads to voluntarily participate in demand-response programs.
quotes: we do not support requiring curtailability of Data Center load as a condition to expedited interconnection of large loads, whether such large loads are Co-Located Loads or stand-alone large loads.

Excluding such applications of Data Centers and AI from expedited interconnection approval, because such applications are unable to be curtailed, would not benefit the public interest and would be harmful to the public interest, which we believe is served by expediting and encouraging the development and application of such Data Centers, AI, and other similarly high-reliability large loads.

Commission guidance should ensure that the owners and operators of the transmission system advise and encourage all large loads, especially Data Centers, of the benefits available to them from demand-response programs.

letters.desc: LPPC accepts curtailability as a factor in study sequencing but opposes using it as an inflexible override, and insists any curtailment and dispatch programs for retail-level load remain within state and LSE authority.
quotes: Establishing an inflexible priority for load and resources that agree to curtail within a cluster study can disadvantage other projects and introduce additional uncertainty for costs and timing of needed generation and network upgrades.
Any expedited treatment for curtailable load and hybrid facilities should not come at the expense of interconnecting historical, native load.

letters.desc: The filer recognises data centres as potential flexibility assets through workload shifting and demand response, and supports contractual flexibility requirements. However, it notes that industry opposed mandatory flexible connections proposed by PJM on legal and reliability grounds, suggesting flexibility obligations should be balanced with operational concerns.
quotes: data centres can be a source of flexibility for the energy grid in the UK. Knittel et al make a similar argument for the USA.
both Data Centres and Supplier companies in the USA have opposed a proposed imposition of flexible connections by the PJM citing legality, fairness and grid reliability.

Data centres could negotiate bespoke contracts with network owners and/or operators, under regulatory approval. These contracts could be used to get the data centres to contribute to the local network to the best of its ability and could result in lower costs for the energy company and lower risks for other grid users.

our key recommendation is that reforms should be designed as a coherent package: queue management, cost allocation, flexibility incentives and socio-environmental screening work best cohesively, rather than introduced separately.

letters.org: National Association of State Utility Consumer Advocates
letters.desc: NASUCA and allied consumer advocates are cautious about curtailment as a reliability tool. Curtailment should not be offered as an interconnection option until enforcement mechanisms, penalty structures, and customer-protection measures are fully developed. When offered, any expedited processing must be contingent on verifiable, telemetry-backed curtailment commitments.
quotes: curtailment should not be considered as a potential option unless and until the mechanisms to implement curtailment are developed—i.e., system protections, the costs as well as penalties resulting from curtailment, and the risks to other customers.
making expedited processing contingent on enforceable curtailment and dispatchability commitment verified through telemetry and subject to penalties for non-performance.

letters.org: Southern Environmental Law CenterAppalachian VoicesNorth Carolina Sustainable Energy Association ,South Carolina Coastal Conservation League ,Southern Alliance for Clean Energy ,
letters.desc: The filers acknowledge that large load demand flexibility can reduce transmission and generation capacity needs and support encouraging or requiring it. However, they oppose offering expedited interconnection as an exchange because current timelines are already years-long and 60-day study windows are not achievable without harming existing queue participants.
quotes: the Commission must be realistic about interconnection timelines.  Currently, large load interconnection can take up to several years in some regions.  Although not perfectly comparable, generation interconnection wait times can also take several years.  Even if flexible interconnection limits the necessary network upgrades, it is simply unrealistic to expect transmission providers to complete interconnection studies for large loads in 60 days.

letters.desc: Vantage supports the goal of expedited study for curtailable loads but warns that requiring hybrid generation to be fully dispatchable undermines the reliability rationale for on-site generation. Curtailment conditions should be developed collaboratively and account for data center customers' need for uninterruptible power. Demand response structures are preferable to direct utility dispatch of hybrid generation.
quotes: Vantage emphasizes that the specific principles and reforms concerning (1) hybrid interconnecting data center facilities supported in whole or in part by dedicated generating facilities (Principles 3 and 5), (2) expedited interconnection study procedures (Principle 7), (3) cost allocation for interconnection-related network upgrades (Principle 8), and (4) a fair and structured transition that respects existing rights (Principle 13) are of greatest importance.

Vantage supports the objective of proposed ANOPR Principle 7 but encourages the Commission's cautious and thoughtful consideration of potential negative consequences of premature implementation of this Principle's dispatchability aspect.

making the generation associated with hybrid facilities fully dispatchable (even if restricted only to grid emergencies) undermines the reliability rationale for installing that generation in the first place.

A key determinant in securing such flexibility will hinge on the conditions of curtailment, which must be further developed through a collaborative process that addresses the economic and reliability concerns of data center customers, as well as those of electric utilities and retail electricity consumers.

letters.desc: The Alliance supports grid reliability goals behind curtailment provisions but opposes any expedited pathway that tips the queue in favor of privately owned or better-capitalized projects. Tribal developers already face structural barriers that limit project redesign within tight timelines.
quotes: Expediting interconnection applications for curtailable projects has the potential to inadvertently tip the scales in favor of privately-owned or better-capitalized projects.

The Alliance therefore calls on the Commission to clarify that expediting interconnection studies for curtailable or dispatchable facilities will not alter the established queue order or delay non-curtailable Tribal projects.

letters.desc: ATC opposes the curtailability concept for expedited study because MISO treats all network load as firm service, meaning operators cannot selectively shed one customer's load ahead of another's. Introducing curtailable large load could force other firm customers to be shed first, creating compliance and fairness problems.
quotes: in ATC's experience, these large load customers require 24/7, uninterrupted, guaranteed, reliable service.  From ATC's perspective, these customers will have network service, and pursuant to MISO's Tariff, all network load is generally treated as firm service.  Introducing curtailment of network load complicates system management and could create scenarios where other customers' firm load is shed before the 'curtailable' large load.

letters.desc: The CPUC contends that commitments by large loads to curtail or shift can be integrated into transmission and resource adequacy planning through existing state constructs, making a new federal framework for expediting flexible loads unnecessary.
quotes: the benefits of curtailment and load shifting commitments can be realized at the state level without federal oversight of retail large load energizations.

letters.desc: FirstEnergy argues that netting load with generation hides real-world variability and control-system interactions that a net number cannot capture. Reliability standards require separate study of load and generation regardless of on-site generation.
quotes: Studying the net impact of hybrid facilities undermines the North American Electric Reliability Corporation ("NERC") transmission planning performance standards, which require testing the ability of the transmission system to withstand specific contingencies including loss of load and loss of generation.
netting fails to provide the redundant protection necessary for the system to perform reliably.

if the transmission network is only planned to support the net withdrawal and export at the point of interconnection, the interconnection capability may be undersized compared to the amount of generation that could be made available at a time when the load customer is curtailed or not consuming power.
Protective equipment that would enforce a net amount is not a failsafe; to the contrary, such equipment suffers from an approximately 6% failure rate.
contingencies and control failures routinely defeat netting.

letters.desc: The filing is skeptical of curtailment as a reliability or interconnection tool. It cites technical barriers including ramp-down speed, voltage stability risks, and the difficulty of enforcing targeted curtailment through distribution utilities outside federal jurisdiction.
quotes: large load projects create significant risks, including the risks of: (1) insufficient supply to meet existing demand and the additional demand of large load projects, (2) skyrocketing prices both in response to insufficient supply and to provide "incentives" in the hope that increased generator revenues will cause them to build sufficient generation to meet the large load demand, and (3) electricity shortages leading to blackouts or "load shed."

new large load contracts with generators who currently serve the aggregate load of electricity customers throughout the country, from residential customers to major industrial load, will siphon power from the grid and leave customers who rely on the bulk power system vulnerable to scarcity pricing and possible shortages and blackouts.

Curtailment of load should not be considered a factor or option when connecting large loads before the mechanisms to implement curtailment including system protections, the costs as well as penalties resulting from curtailment, and the risks to other customers are fully considered and incorporated into any curtailment provision.

letters.desc: Maryland opposes any FERC action that constrains state authority over demand response, virtual power plants, distributed generation, behind-the-meter resources, and energy efficiency programs essential to affordability and reliability.
quotes: FERC actions should not exacerbate affordability and reliability issues, nor constrain state actions on resource decisions, demand response, virtual power plants (VPPs), distributed generation, behind-the-meter generation and energy efficiency

letters.desc: The Maryland PSC opposes curtailment-based expediting if it allows load growth to outstrip supply additions, warning of more frequent critical system conditions and off-peak price increases for non-large-load customers.
quotes: if a significant amount of curtailment is incentivized and implemented such that new large loads are added to the system faster than new generation can come online, a growing number of customers would be leaning on a relatively stagnant supply of electricity. This would mean that critical system conditions could be approached more frequently and reliability would be challenged more often.

letters.desc: The Monitor rejects demand-side options including demand response and PRD as viable substitutes for generation capacity, citing weak performance incentives, a high PRD strike price cap, and the absence of non-performance penalties outside PAI events.
quotes: If large new data center loads want an expedited interconnection process, loads should be required to bring their own new generation.
In their current and proposed forms, demand side solutions offer no viable substitution for generation capacity resources.

letters.desc: The filing argues that curtailable load and demand-side resources are not a viable alternative to generation capacity. Data centers in practice resist meaningful curtailment, PRD strike prices are too high to serve as real demand resources, and adding large loads without generation will drive up energy and capacity prices.
quotes: In their current and proposed forms, demand side solutions offer no viable substitution for generation capacity resources.

If 20,000 MW of new data center load were added and 90 percent or less of this load were offered in the capacity market as emergency demand side resources, the Market Monitor estimates that the increased cost of capacity would be around $5.48 billion per year to existing customers.

letters.desc: Recent SPP actions and the HILL process mitigate the need for FERC intervention. The HILL process expedites interconnection of large loads with firm transmission service when generation exists today. SPP has already filed its procedures with FERC and should not be forced to redevelop them under a federal one-size-fits-all mandate.
quotes: recent actions taken by the Southwest Power Pool (SPP) to address this issue mitigate the need for FERC's intervention
The HILL process was designed to expedite the interconnection of large loads taking firm transmission service when there is sufficient generation on the system today.

the Secretary's requested reforms are unnecessary. The necessary steps to ensure the goal of timely, orderly and nondiscriminatory interconnection of new large loads are already being taken, and are expected to be accomplished in the SPP's operating area without the need for FERC's intervention.

SPP has been proactive in the development of such procedures and should not have to develop an entirely new process designed as a one-size-fits-all approach that may provide only marginal differences from what SPP has developed and already filed with FERC.

letters.org: North Carolina Utilities Commission Public Staff
letters.desc: The ANOPR's special accommodation for load that agrees to be curtailed quickly infringes state jurisdiction. The filing wants states to keep their ability to set flexibility requirements rather than have FERC impose them.
quotes: The ANOPR proposal to provide special accommodation to load that agrees to be curtailed is an example of a rule that quickly infringes on state jurisdiction.
limit[ing] States’ ability to implement pro ability to implement protective measures, such as large load tariffs and flexibility requirements

letters.desc: The PA PUC warns that ANOPR proposals could preempt state-level flexibility requirements for large loads, limiting state commissions' ability to manage large load impacts on the grid.
quotes: The proposals in the ANOPR could limit a state's ability to implement protective measures, such as large load tariffs and flexibility requirements.

letters.desc: PJM warns that allowing curtailable large loads to receive expedited study without firm deliverability analysis shifts reliability burdens to real-time operations and could result in frequent real-time interruptions, undermining the "five nines" reliability that data centers require.
quotes: the proposed reforms appear to signal an openness to a less-reliable planning paradigm for new generation facilities (see, e.g., Principles 3 and 5) where hybrid facilities involving "new generation facilities" are studied based solely on injection and/or withdrawal rights requested, and large loads and hybrid facilities that agree to be curtailable will have their studies expedited so that such facilities can be put into operation with greater speed.
Has this tradeoff between reliability and speed to market been sufficiently vetted, and are the potential costs documented and understood?

The "connect-and-manage" framework could lead to future grid build out that is not as robust and reliable as the planning standard PJM (and other RTOs/ISOs) have adhered to for decades if voluntarily curtailable load (Principle 7) is not planned for as firm load in regional transmission planning processes.

letters.org: Southwest Power Pool Transmission Owner Group
letters.desc: The SPP TO Group consistently argues that FERC should not issue a one-size-fits-all rule and should instead give RTOs and ISOs broad flexibility under the independent entity variation standard. SPP's HILL and CPP reforms are offered as proof that regional stakeholder processes can satisfy every ANOPR principle without mandated standardization.
quotes: the Commission should avoid issuing an overly prescriptive rule, but should instead provide broad latitude for transmission providers and their stakeholders to develop their own solutions to the challenges posed by large load interconnections.
Standardization is merely a tool to achieve that end; it is not an end in itself.

A final rule in this proceeding should not undermine the extraordinary progress the SPP region has made by disturbing the carefully balanced consensus reforms that SPP, its public and investor-owned Load Serving Entities, and state regulators have collaborated to develop.

the Commission should 'expressly state that RTOs and ISOs will have broad flexibility to seek variations from any pro forma tariff adopted by the Commission under the independent entity variation standard.'

While a 20 MW threshold may work for other regions, it would not work for SPP.  However, transmission providers outside of SPP should be left to define 'large loads' as they see fit with their stakeholders and according to their region's unique circumstances.  The Commission need not dictate what the limit is, although it should direct all transmission providers to designate and justify an appropriate threshold.

The withdrawal penalty framework SPP has embraced satisfies Principle 4, and the Commission should not impose a new rule that interferes with what SPP and its stakeholders have accomplished.  The SPP TO Group remains agnostic as to the appropriate size of withdrawal penalties in other regions so long as they accomplish the ANOPR's intent to deter speculative projects.
The SPP TO Group strongly support CHILLS and recommends that the Commission approve that proposal as a valuable, region-specific means of expediting curtailable load interconnections.

CPP shows that stakeholders wish to, and are capable of, designing interconnection solutions that work for their specific regional needs without encroaching on state jurisdiction.  By allowing transmission providers to develop their own region-specific interconnection solutions, the Commission can avoid the jurisdictional minefield that an overbroad rule might create.

letters.org: Utility Intervention Unit, New York State Department of Stat
letters.desc: The UIU argues that curtailability and dispatchability do not substitute for firm capacity. Flexible load creates forecasting uncertainty, gaming potential, and extreme-weather reliability risks that must be managed with enforceable performance metrics, not queue priority.
quotes: UIU rejects the ANOPRs premise that large loads that agree to be curtailable and hybrid facilities that agree to be curtailable and dispatchable should be expedited.
A customer receiving interconnection priority for being curtailable but failing to perform could expose consumers to higher costs and reliability risks.
